The original dataset provides whether the student was a basic participant, basic concentrator, basic completor, and/or a centrentrator 150 when taking a CTE course. It looks like each observation is unique by grade of the student. This means that one PersonID can have multiple observations.
In order to determine how I want to organize this data so that each observation represents the full characteristics of each PersonID I need to understand how these values are defined.

Basic Participant: Any grade 9-12 student who successfully completes one or more state-approved CTE course(s).
Basic Concentrator: this is the old standard for years and required the student complete 240 hours. Any student successfully enrolled in a single CTE field for more than 240 hours (successful is defined as passing grade).
Basic Completor: any concentrator who attains academic and technical knowledge and skills and graduates from high school.
Concentrator 150: This is the new standard - Any grade 9-12 student who successfully completes 150+ course hours (or more) as part of a state-approved secondary CTE program, within one career field.

Judging by these definitions, it seems that we will want three categories;

Those that participated in a CTE course but were not a concentrator or a completor, and
Those that participated in a CTE course and graduated as a concentrator.
Those that did not participate in a CTE course.

So essentially, filtering this dataset to provide the “highest level achieved” in terms of CTE coursework. We will focus on filtering this dataset to the highest level achieved and will then join with the graduate list which will have all the individuals that did not participate in any CTE courses.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Interpretation of findings
Immediate postsecondary enrollment within one year of high school graduation is shaped by a combination of individual, school-level, and academic preparation factors.
From a demographic perspective, the strongest influences were special education status and economic status. Students who had received special education services and those who were economically disadvantaged were substantially less likely to attend immediately, suggesting barriers related to academic support needs and financial resources. Race/ethnicity also played a role, with Asian/PI and White students having the highest rates and American Indian students the lowest, reflecting broader systemic disparities.
High school characteristics added another layer of influence. Economic conditions in the community—particularly lower unemployment rates and higher wages relative to the state average—were more strongly associated with immediate enrollment than rurality alone. While urban students had slightly higher attendance rates than their rural counterparts, community economic health appeared to be the more critical driver, potentially reflecting both the local opportunity structure and the resources available to schools and families.
High school accomplishments showed the most direct and consistent relationship with postsecondary entry. Strong academic performance (ACT and MCA scores) and early college exposure through PSEO were powerful predictors of immediate enrollment, with PSEO standing out as the single strongest individual factor. In contrast, greater engagement in Career and Technical Education was linked to lower immediate enrollment, likely reflecting alternative workforce-oriented pathways.
Taken together, these findings suggest that academic readiness, early exposure to college, and favorable economic contexts all facilitate rapid postsecondary transition, while financial, academic support, and systemic equity barriers can slow or divert that path. At the same time, CTE participation highlights that not all students aim for immediate college enrollment—emphasizing the importance of supporting multiple, equally viable pathways into adulthood.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Rank of variable importance

PSEO participation

Why: Strongest effect size (Cramer’s V=0.356) and largest differences in immediate postsecondary attendance (81.4% vs. 46.8% for non-participants).
Interpretation: Clear indicator of college readiness and momentum toward rapid postsecondary entry.

Special education status

Why: Second-highest effect size (Cramer’s V=0.282) with a large gap in attendance (67.9% vs. 29.5%).
Interpretation: Indicates substantial barriers for students with special education needs.

ACT Composite Score

Why: Very large F-value (2827.0) and substantial mean score differences between groups (up to 3 points).
Interpretation: Strong measure of academic readiness and predictor of immediate enrollment.

Economic status

Why: Moderate effect size (Cramer’s V=0.225) and large gap (70% vs. 46.7%).
Interpretation: Reflects the role of financial resources in enabling postsecondary transition.

MCA scores (Math, Reading, Science)

Why: All had very large F-values (4,000–6,000+) with consistent gaps favoring completers.
Interpretation: Reinforces that academic performance across core subjects correlates with postsecondary entry.

Average county unemployment rate

Why: Largest F-value among school characteristics (575.6) and clear differences in economic contexts between completers and non-completers.
Interpretation: Suggests broader labor market conditions may influence postsecondary decisions.

Average wages (percent of state)

Why: Strong F-value (324.7) and consistent pattern of higher wages linked to higher attendance.
Interpretation: Captures local economic strength and opportunity.

Race/Ethnicity

Why: Smaller effect size (Cramer’s V=0.113) but notable disparities across groups.
Interpretation: Points to systemic inequities that affect postsecondary access.

CTE achievement level

Why: Weak association (Cramer’s V=0.071) but reverse pattern—higher involvement linked to lower immediate enrollment.
Interpretation: Likely reflects intentional workforce-oriented pathways.

Total CTE courses taken

Why: Large F-value (1002.0) but consistent with CTE achievement in direction—more CTE linked to lower immediate enrollment.
Interpretation: Reinforces the CTE–workforce pathway pattern.

RUCA classification

Why: Weakest association (Cramer’s V=0.035) and small differences in rates.
Interpretation: Rurality has limited direct impact once other factors are considered, though it may operate indirectly through economic conditions and access.

Demographics
Here are the variables we will be exploring;

economic.status

Interpretation
Individual demographic characteristics showed meaningful differences in the likelihood of attending postsecondary within one year of high school graduation, with special education status and economic status having the strongest associations. Students who had received special education services and those who were economically disadvantaged were much less likely to make the immediate transition to postsecondary, highlighting potential barriers related to academic support needs and financial resources.
Race/ethnicity was also significantly related to postsecondary attendance, though the differences were smaller in magnitude. Asian/PI and White students had the highest immediate attendance rates, while American Indian students had the lowest. These patterns suggest disparities that may stem from a combination of historical, structural, and resource-related factors influencing access to and navigation of postsecondary pathways.
Taken together, the demographic findings indicate that academic support needs, economic resources, and systemic equity issues all play roles in shaping postsecondary access. Addressing these factors—through targeted supports, financial assistance, and culturally responsive programming—could help close gaps in immediate postsecondary enrollment.

Interpretation
High school context appears to play a meaningful, though varied, role in whether students attend postsecondary within one year of graduation. Community economic conditions—both unemployment rate and wage levels relative to the state average—were more strongly linked to postsecondary attendance than RUCA classification (urban–rural mix). Students from economically stronger areas (lower unemployment, higher wages) were more likely to transition quickly to postsecondary and to complete within the first year.
In contrast, the urban–rural mix of a high school’s location showed only a weak relationship with postsecondary attendance. While entirely urban schools had the highest immediate attendance rates and town/rural mix schools the lowest, the gap was relatively small compared to the economic variables.
These results suggest that economic opportunity in the community where a student attends high school may be a more important driver of immediate postsecondary enrollment and completion than rurality alone. However, the weaker relationship with RUCA also indicates that place still matters, but its effects may operate indirectly—perhaps through economic conditions or access to postsecondary institutions—rather than through rurality itself.

text:

Interpretation
High school accomplishment measures reveal two distinct patterns in immediate postsecondary enrollment. First, indicators of college readiness and academic achievement—such as higher ACT scores, stronger MCA performance in math, reading, and science, and participation in PSEO—are strongly linked to higher rates of attending and completing postsecondary within one year. The particularly strong relationship with PSEO suggests that early exposure to college coursework not only signals readiness but may also build momentum toward rapid postsecondary transition.
Second, greater involvement in Career and Technical Education (CTE)—both in terms of number of courses taken and concentrator/completer status—was associated with lower immediate postsecondary attendance. This may reflect intentional pathway choices, where students prepare for direct workforce entry rather than college, or differences in academic preparation and postsecondary aspirations.
Overall, these findings indicate that college-oriented academic preparation supports immediate postsecondary entry, while career-oriented pathways may divert graduates toward alternative post–high school options. This divergence highlights the importance of aligning supports with students’ chosen pathways—ensuring that those pursuing workforce entry have strong employment prospects, while those aiming for college receive the preparation and early exposure that promotes successful transition.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Interpretation of findings
Postsecondary participation at any point after high school is influenced by a combination of individual demographic factors, the economic and geographic context of the high school, and academic preparation and achievement during high school.
From a demographic perspective, special education status and economic status are the strongest predictors of whether a student ever attends postsecondary. Students who had received special education services and those who were economically disadvantaged were substantially less likely to attend, underscoring the role of resource availability and academic support needs in shaping postsecondary trajectories. Race/ethnicity differences, though smaller in magnitude, still point to systemic inequities, with American Indian students having the lowest participation rates and Asian/PI and White students the highest.
High school characteristics contribute to postsecondary participation, though their influence is more modest compared to demographics and accomplishments. Students from high schools in communities with higher wages relative to the state average were more likely to attend, suggesting a link between local economic prosperity and access to postsecondary education. The small positive relationship with unemployment rate may indicate that fewer local job opportunities encourage more students to seek education beyond high school. Rurality, as measured by RUCA classification, showed only a weak association, suggesting that economic context outweighs location alone in determining eventual postsecondary participation.
High school accomplishments remain the most direct and consistent predictors. Higher ACT and MCA scores in all tested subjects, and especially participation in PSEO, were strongly associated with eventual postsecondary attendance. PSEO participation stands out as the single most powerful academic-related factor, suggesting that early exposure to college coursework creates momentum toward enrollment, even if students delay entry. In contrast, greater involvement in Career and Technical Education—both in number of courses and concentrator/completer status—was linked to lower postsecondary participation, likely reflecting intentional workforce entry pathways.
Taken together, these findings suggest that eventual postsecondary participation is shaped by a complex interplay of personal resources, community context, and academic preparation. Strengthening supports for economically disadvantaged students, students receiving special education services, and underrepresented racial/ethnic groups—while sustaining and expanding opportunities like PSEO—may be key to increasing postsecondary access. At the same time, supporting the success of students pursuing career-oriented high school pathways will be essential to ensuring equitable long-term employment outcomes.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Rank of variable importance
The relative importance of most predictors remained stable when comparing immediate postsecondary attendance to ever attending postsecondary. PSEO participation and special education status consistently ranked as the top two predictors, followed closely by ACT Composite Score. Academic achievement measures (MCA Reading, Math, and Science) maintained strong positions in both timeframes.
Two notable shifts emerged: Total CTE courses rose in importance for ever attendance (ranked 11th to 8th), while average county unemployment rate declined (8th to 11th). These changes suggest that CTE involvement may play a slightly larger role in eventual enrollment than in immediate enrollment, while local unemployment conditions appear less influential over longer time horizons.
Overall, academic readiness, early exposure to college coursework, and key demographic factors remain the most consistent drivers of postsecondary participation, regardless of timing, while some contextual factors shift in influence over time.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Interpretation of findings
When considering all variables together, the largest associations with postsecondary graduation were found in high school accomplishments and demographics, with high school characteristics showing weaker but still significant effects.
Top associations emerged for:

PSEO participation (φ = 0.370) – very strong positive association.
Race/Ethnicity (Cramer’s V = 0.271) – substantial differences across groups.
Special Education status (φ = 0.243) – strong negative association.
Economic status (φ = 0.231) – lower-income students had lower graduation rates.
ACT Composite Score (Δ = +2.95) – large academic performance gap.

Moderate associations included:

MCA scores (Math, Reading, Science: Δ ≈ +0.47 to +0.54).
CTE achievement (Cramer’s V = 0.149) – completers more likely to graduate.
Total CTE courses (Δ = −1.13) – inverse relationship.

Weaker associations appeared in:

High school unemployment rate (Δ = +0.17) – moderate effect.
Rural-urban classification (Cramer’s V = 0.033) – very small effect.
High school average wage level (Δ = +0.005) – minimal practical effect.

Academic readiness and early postsecondary exposure dominate as predictors of postsecondary graduation. PSEO participation stands out as the single strongest correlate, followed closely by ACT performance and MCA scores, signaling that preparation for college-level work during high school is a decisive factor in persistence and completion.
Demographic variables also show meaningful influence: disparities by race/ethnicity, economic status, and special education status indicate that systemic barriers and resource gaps persist well into postsecondary pathways.
High school community context—such as unemployment rates—matters, but less so than individual-level academic factors. The weak relationship with rurality and average wage levels suggests that broader geographic classifications do not strongly dictate completion outcomes once students are enrolled.
CTE pathways present a nuanced picture: while achieving concentrator/completer status correlates with higher graduation rates, a greater volume of CTE coursework is linked to lower completion, perhaps indicating divergence toward employment-focused rather than degree-focused trajectories.
Overall, the data point to a layered structure of influence, with academic preparation and early college engagement as the most actionable levers, demographic disparities as structural challenges, and community context as a secondary but notable factor.

Across all three outcomes—postsecondary graduation (ps.grad), attendance within one year of high school graduation (attended.ps.within.1yr), and eventual postsecondary attendance (attended.ps)—the rank ordering of predictors is remarkably consistent. PSEO participation, special education status, ACT Composite Score, and economic status consistently emerge as the four strongest predictors, suggesting these factors play a dominant role both in access to and completion of postsecondary education.
The middle tier predictors—MCA Reading, MCA Math, MCA Science, CTE achievement, and race/ethnicity—show moderate but stable associations across outcomes. These likely represent broader academic preparation and demographic context effects that influence persistence but are secondary to the top-tier variables.
The lowest tier predictors—total CTE courses taken, rural–urban descriptor, average unemployment rate, and average wages as a percentage of the state average—show weak and consistent rankings, suggesting that community context and broad CTE exposure have limited predictive power once individual academic and program participation variables are considered.
Overall, the stability of the ranking across outcomes underscores that the same core student-level factors drive both early postsecondary participation and eventual degree completion, while community and school context exert comparatively smaller effects.

Interpretation
Across the three demographic indicators—economic status, race/ethnicity, and special education status—special education status emerged as the strongest predictor of postsecondary graduation (φ = 0.243). Students receiving special education services had significantly lower graduation rates (13.4%) than their peers (47.1%), reflecting the largest proportional gap.
Economic status was the second-strongest factor (φ = 0.231). Students from lower economic backgrounds graduated at less than half the rate of higher-income peers (25.9% vs. 50.1%), underscoring the continued influence of socioeconomic barriers on degree attainment.
Race/ethnicity also showed a meaningful association (Cramer’s V = 0.271), though its pattern was more complex. Asian/Pacific Islander students had the highest graduation rate (43.7%), while American Indian students had the lowest (15.8%), with Black, Hispanic, and White students falling in between. These differences point to both systemic disparities and potential cultural or institutional factors affecting graduation likelihood.
Overall, while all three variables are significantly associated with graduation outcomes, special education status and economic status represent the most direct and consistent barriers, whereas race/ethnicity patterns suggest both concentrated disadvantages for some groups and relative advantages for others.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Interpretation of findings
Top Associations

Economic Status – Strongly differentiates sectors, with lower-income students overrepresented in Public 2-year institutions and higher-income students in Public 4-year institutions.
Special Education Status – Strong association; students with special education experience are much more likely to graduate from Public 2-year institutions.
ACT Composite Score – Largest academic gap across sectors; 4-year graduates score highest, 2-year lowest, “Other” in between.
PSEO Participation – Significantly higher among Public 4-year graduates, lowest in Public 2-year sector.
CTE Achievement – Strong, inverse pattern to PSEO; highest among Public 2-year graduates, lowest in Public 4-year sector.

Moderate Associations

Race/Ethnicity – Distinct group distributions, with White and Asian/Pacific Islander graduates concentrated in the 4-year sector, and Black and Hispanic graduates more prevalent in Public 2-year and “Other” sectors.
MCA Scores (Math, Reading, Science) – Consistent sector hierarchy favoring 4-year graduates, but slightly smaller gaps than ACT Composite Score.
Total CTE Courses Taken – Higher among Public 2-year graduates, lower in Public 4-year graduates, mirroring CTE achievement patterns.
Dem_Desc (Geographic Background) – Urban students more represented in 4-year sector; town/rural backgrounds more common in 2-year sector.

Weak Associations

Average Unemployment Rate – Lower rates linked to higher likelihood of graduating from Public 4-year institutions, but effect size is small.
Average Wages (% of State Median) – Similar pattern to unemployment rate; statistically significant but minor differences across sectors.

The sector of graduation reflects a sorting process shaped most strongly by socioeconomic status, academic preparation, and high school program participation. High-income, academically strong students with greater exposure to advanced coursework (e.g., PSEO) are more likely to graduate from Public 4-year institutions. Students from lower-income households or with stronger vocational preparation through CTE tend toward Public 2-year institutions. Demographic background and local economic conditions matter, but less so than direct academic and programmatic experiences.

Interpretation
When focusing only on college graduates, SpecialEdStatus emerges as the strongest demographic predictor of institution type, with a clear preference for Public 2-year colleges among graduates with special education backgrounds. This is a sharper pattern than in earlier, unfiltered analyses, suggesting that once enrolled, special education students are more likely to complete in 2-year settings than to persist through 4-year institutions.
Economic Status remains important but is no longer dominant; higher-income students are still more likely to graduate from Public 4-year institutions, while lower-income students are split between Public 2-year and “Other” institutions.
Race/Ethnicity differences persist, but are more nuanced — Public 4-year colleges have particularly high shares of Black and Asian/PI graduates, Public 2-year colleges have high representation of AI and Unknown, while “Other” institutions capture a diverse mix without a dominant racial or ethnic group.
Overall, compared to the broader population analysis, demographic factors show a more balanced influence here, with SpecialEdStatus overtaking Economic Status as the primary differentiator of graduation sector among completers.

Unemployment rate and especially relative wages — play a stronger role in distinguishing between graduation sectors. The wage-based stratification is particularly clear: graduates from higher-wage communities are far more likely to attend and graduate from a public 4-year institution, while those from lower-wage areas are more concentrated in the public 2-year sector. This suggests that, even when looking only at college graduates, local economic conditions remain a strong influence on the type of institution attended, with rural and lower-income areas channeling more students toward 2-year programs.

text:

Here are the variables we will explore.

pseo.participant

MCA.M
MCA.R
MCA.S


Interpretation
Taken together, these findings suggest that graduation sector is closely aligned with distinct high school academic and programmatic profiles. Public 4-year graduates generally exhibit stronger standardized test performance and greater engagement with advanced academic pathways like PSEO, while public 2-year graduates are more likely to concentrate in CTE pathways and demonstrate lower average performance on academic achievement measures. The “Other” sector occupies a middle ground, reflecting a more heterogeneous mix of academic preparation and program participation. This alignment between pre-college academic profile and graduation sector underscores the enduring influence of high school performance and course-taking patterns on postsecondary outcomes.

ACTCompositeScorepseo.participantcte.achievementtotal.cte.courses.takenMCA.MMCA.RMCA.S

The effect size here is substantial, suggesting ACT scores may be one of the most powerful predictors of institution sector, even after filtering to college graduates only.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Interpretation of findings
When comparing across demographics, high school characteristics, and high school accomplishments, the strongest differentiators of postsecondary graduation location are academic performance measures (ACTCompositeScore, MCA Math, Reading, and Science). These consistently show large and statistically significant gaps, with out-of-state graduates performing highest, followed by in-state graduates, and regional graduates lowest.
Demographic variables—particularly economic status—show moderate associations, indicating that higher-income students are more likely to graduate outside their high school region or out-of-state, while lower-income students more often remain in-region. Race/ethnicity and special education status have weaker but still significant associations, showing that location differences exist across groups but are less pronounced than for economic status.
High school characteristics like community type (urban/town/rural mix), average local unemployment rate, and wage levels show moderate associations, suggesting that local economic and geographic context influences whether students remain in-region or seek education further away.
Overall, academic achievement emerges as the most powerful differentiator of graduation location, followed by socioeconomic and geographic context, while other demographic factors contribute more modestly. This mirrors patterns observed in earlier variables such as ps.grad and ps.grad.InstitutionSector, but here the test score measures dominate more strongly, and associations with demographic background are generally weaker than in those earlier analyses.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Demographics
Here are the variables we will be exploring;

economic.status
RaceEthnicity
SpecialEdStatus


Interpretation
Graduates’ postsecondary location choices show clear socioeconomic and mobility patterns. Lower-income individuals are more likely to remain in-region, reflecting potential financial or access constraints, while higher-income graduates display greater geographic mobility, particularly toward out-of-state completions. Racial and ethnic differences are present but smaller in magnitude, with Asian/PI and Hispanic graduates having more balanced distributions between in-region and other Minnesota institutions, while Black and White graduates lean more toward in-region completions. Special education graduates exhibit the strongest in-region concentration and the lowest out-of-state rates, suggesting more limited mobility compared to peers. Overall, the associations observed here are weaker than in prior analyses of postsecondary outcomes, indicating that demographic factors are less determinative of where graduates complete their degrees compared to whether they complete them at all.

economic.statusRaceEthnicitySpecialEdStatus


Associations: Cramer’s V = 0.101 (χ² = 507.534, df = 2, p < 0.001) indicates a small but statistically significant relationship between economic status and postsecondary graduation location among graduates. Higher-income individuals are more likely to graduate from out-of-state institutions (20.6% vs. 12.9% for lower-income). Lower-income individuals are more likely to graduate from a college in their high school region (36.9% vs. 27.4% for higher-income). The share graduating from a Minnesota institution outside their home region is similar between income groups (about 50%).
Interpretation: Economic status has a modest influence on postsecondary graduation location among graduates. Lower-income graduates tend to remain closer to home, with over a third staying in their high school region, while higher-income graduates display more geographic mobility, especially toward out-of-state institutions. Similar rates of graduation in other parts of Minnesota suggest that the main difference lies in the ability or willingness to leave the state entirely.

Overall, high school context appears to influence where students graduate more than economic measures do, but all associations in this section are weaker than those observed for broader educational attainment variables in prior analyses. By contrast, CTE participation and achievement appear less tied to postsecondary graduation location, reflecting that career and technical pathways may be more evenly distributed geographically or less dependent on academic performance metrics. title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Interpretation Across All Analyses
Your analyses across attended.ps.within.first.year.hsgrad, attended.ps, ps.grad, ps.grad.location, and ps.grad.InstitutionSector converge on a clear story: postsecondary pathways, especially the type and location of college attendance and graduation, strongly shape long-term employment outcomes.

1. Academic preparation is rising as a key differentiator.
The most striking finding is the surge in ACT Composite Score as a top predictor for where and what type of institution students graduate from. This shift suggests that academic readiness now plays a bigger role than family income in determining postsecondary patterns, especially when looking beyond “did they graduate” to “where did they graduate from.”
For workforce engagement, this implies:

Students with higher academic readiness are more likely to leave the local region (out-of-state or outside their high school region) and attend 4-year institutions — potentially making them harder to retain locally.
Local workforce strategies need to consider how to connect academically strong students to in-region career opportunities early, before they are “pulled away” by academic mobility.



2. Economic status still matters — but differently now.
In earlier models (overall participation and graduation), Economic Status was consistently the top predictor. In the location- and sector-based analyses, it dropped several spots.

This means income is less about whether students succeed in postsecondary education, and more about the type of postsecondary pathway they choose.
Lower-income students are more concentrated in public 2-year colleges — which tend to be closer to home and linked to local employment pipelines.

For workforce planning:

Public 2-year pathways are a prime engagement point for students from lower-income backgrounds — this is where targeted partnerships, apprenticeships, and “earn while you learn” models could have high impact.



3. Local economic conditions influence mobility decisions.
Average Unemployment Rate rose in importance for ps.grad.location and ps.grad.InstitutionSector, suggesting that students’ decisions about where to attend/graduate are shaped by job market health.

Higher unemployment in home regions may push students toward other areas for school — and potentially for work afterward.
Conversely, strong local economies may retain more students in local or regional institutions.

This underscores the importance of making local job opportunities visible to students during high school, not just after graduation.


4. CTE and PSEO matter more for pathway type than for location retention.
Career & Technical Education (CTE) and PSEO participation have moderate influence in sector-based models, but remain lower-ranked overall.

PSEO tends to correlate with 4-year public graduation, while CTE is more evenly distributed but strongest in 2-year institutions.
These programs may be less about keeping students local and more about shaping the kind of postsecondary credential they earn.

The implication:

To retain students locally, align CTE pathways with local industry demand and connect PSEO experiences to in-region internships or mentorships.



5. The mobility-retention challenge is real.
Across analyses, a pattern emerges:

High academic readiness + higher income → higher likelihood of out-of-state or outside-region graduation (and thus risk of workforce loss).
Lower income + CTE focus → higher likelihood of 2-year local or regional graduation (and thus stronger potential for workforce retention).

If the goal is to engage high school students in the local workforce, the strategies may need to be dual-tracked:

Retention Track: Strengthen the connection between 2-year programs and local employers, with pathways that lead to strong wages and advancement without needing to leave the area.
Return Track: For students likely to leave (high ACT, 4-year, out-of-state), create strong alumni networks, internships, and “boomerang” incentives to bring them back post-graduation.

Bottom line:

This analysis confirms that postsecondary type and location are the levers that matter most for workforce engagement. Academic readiness now rivals — and in some cases surpasses — family income as a driver of where students go after high school. Local workforce strategy should therefore focus on making both academic and career pathways visible, valuable, and connected to the region — with different engagement tactics for students on different trajectories.

The next dataset is individuals that were enrolled in CTE courses. I’m first going to load the entire dataset, then clean it up, and then I will merge it with my master/Central graduate dataset.

         cte.year = ifelse(is.na(Introduced) & is.na(Discontinued), 2021, cte.year),

title: CTEEnrollment
section: Summary - Number of CTE courses taken by a student
text:
Summary - Number of CTE courses taken by a student

We’ll start with summarising the number of cte courses the observations have taken.
The tables below show that the average number of CTE courses taken by all PersonID in the master dataset is 4.06 with a standard deviation of +/-3.72. This is a high standard deviation meaning there are values quite far from the mean.
The second row of the table shows the average number of CTE courses taken by individuals who took at least one CTE course. The average jumps up a bit to 4.84 with a standard deviation of 3.56.








Below is a chart showing the distribution of CTE courses taken by individuals. This shows that a a large majority of students take 10 courses or less.








Up next is to see if the percentage of students taking a CTE course varies significantly by RUCA group.
There is a significant difference in whether a student has taken at least one CTE course and their high school county RUCA category. Although 84% of all graduates took at least one CTE course, that percentage is highest in urban/town/rural mix counties with 85%.
Of those students that took at least 1 CTE course, the average number of CTE courses taken ranged from 5.1 in our entirely urban districts to 4.6 in town/rural mix districts.

title: CTEEnrollment
section: Summary - CareerCluster of CTE courses taken
text:
Summary - CareerCluster of CTE courses taken
Let’s dig into the breadth of CTE course concentrations a graduate would take by looking at the proportion of graduates that took at least one course within a concentration.
The table below shows that a third of all graduates took a CTE course in Transportation, Distribution & Logistics, and Human Services, followed by 27% in Manufacturing, and 25% in each Agriculture, Food and Natural Resources.


cte.cf.prop <- master.4 %>%
  gather(key = "CareerCluster", value = "n.courses", `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  mutate(cte.cf.taken = ifelse(n.courses > 0, "Yes", "No")) %>%
  tabyl(CareerCluster, cte.cf.taken) %>%
  mutate(pct.taken.cf = Yes / (Yes + No)) %>% 
  arrange(desc(pct.taken.cf))

datatable(cte.cf.prop, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE,
          options = list(scrollX = TRUE)) %>%
  formatCurrency(2:3, "", digits = 0) %>%
  formatPercentage(4)






Now we will take a look at the breakdown of the number of times a CTE courses has been taken within a CareerCluster for each PersonID. I expect there to be a lot of variation in this data since different schools might focus on different types of CTE offerings depending on the local employment makeup.
First, lets look at the concentrations of courses taken across CareerClusters.
Surprisingly, agriculture, food and natural resources was the careercluster with the highest percentage of courses taken with 15.9%. This was followed by human services with 13.4% and then transportation, distribution and logistics with 12.6% of CTE courses taken in that CareerCluster.








Lets see how this looks broken down by county.
The county maps do show some differences in percentages across career clusters. Agriculture, food and natural resources had higher percentages taken in the western and central counties. Manufacturing was taken at a higher percentage in the northern and southern counties. Human services and transportation, distribution & logistics was pretty standard across all.

We have 5,744,192 rows and 5 columns in this dataset. Here are the descriptions for each of the columns.

K12AsstTimeID: Day, month, and year the assessment took place.
TestName: Name of the test taken. There are 12 different tests in the dataset -

ACCESS: English proficiency,
ALTACCESS: English proficiency for special education or meet requirements
MCA-II & MCA-III: Minnesota Comprehsensive Assessments (series 2 and 3)
MOD-II, MOD-III: Modified Comprehensive Assessment, used only until 2014
MTAS & MTAS-III: Minnesota Test of Academic Skills
MTELL: an alternate assessment for students learning English (like the MTAS or MOD). MTELL was only administered from 2007-2010 during the series-II of MCAs.
SOLOM: Minnesota Student Oral Language Observation Matrix
TEAE: one of two assessments that Minnesota used to meet the requirements to test ELs in all four domains of language (the other was SOLOM). TEAE was used 2002 until we changed to ACCESS in 2012. SOLOM was used 2004 until we changed to ACCESS in 2012.

Subject: Classifies each test that is given to a student based on the areas measured. There are 8 factors;

A: Aural (listening) - ACCESS & ALTACCESS only
C: Composite - ACCESS & ALTACCESS only
L: Listening/Speaking
M: Math
O: Oral - ACCESS & ALTACCESS only
R: Reading
S: Science
W: Writing

GradeTested: Grade student was enrolled in when performing assessment.
AchievementLevel: Used to count the number of students in each achievement level by group such as race, gender, and ethnicity. It must be calculated from other students at a similar graden and subject for a specific year.

ACCESS students are graded on a language proficiency scale of 1 through 6.
ALT-ACCESS students are graded using a P1 through P3 and A1 through A3 scale.
There are 4 different levels for the MCA test

D: Does not meet standards
E: Exceeds standards
M: Meets Standards
P: Partially meets standards

SOLOM tests are 1-5 scale with 5 being the highest
TEAE tests are 1-5 scale with 5 being the highest.


There are two ways in which we are going to code our graduates.
The first is to identify whether a student has been identified as an English learner. This means filtering students that have taken the ACCESS, ALT-ACCESS, MTELL, MTAS, TEAE, MOD-II, MOD-III, or SOLOM at least once in their career.
The second is be determining their highest achievement level in each subject of the MCA tests within the dataset. The dataset provides each instance of a test for each student so many are students are listed numerous times - once for each time they took a test.
Lets do this in two separate files and then join each with the master file.
Starting with identifying the EL students.


el <- assessments.original %>%
  filter(!TestName %in% c("MCA-II", "MCA-III")) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(PersonID) %>%
  mutate(english.learner = 1)

This dataset identified 34,995 individuals who were identified as an english learner at least one time in the original dataset.
Now we will determine the highest achievement level for each subject for each student.


mca <- assessments.original %>%
  filter(TestName %in% c("MCA-II", "MCA-III")) %>%
  filter(AchievementLevel != "NULL") %>%
  droplevels() %>%
  mutate(AchievementLevelCode = ifelse(AchievementLevel == "D", 1,
                                       ifelse(AchievementLevel == "P", 2,
                                              ifelse(AchievementLevel == "M", 3, 4))))

mca.highest <- mca %>%
  group_by(PersonID, Subject) %>%
  filter(AchievementLevelCode == max(AchievementLevelCode)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(PersonID, Subject, AchievementLevelCode) %>%
  mutate(mca.subject = paste("MCA.", Subject, sep = "")) %>%
  select(PersonID, mca.subject, AchievementLevelCode) %>%
  mutate(id = seq(n())) %>%
  spread(key = mca.subject, value = AchievementLevelCode) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  fill(MCA.M, .direction = c("downup")) %>%
  fill(MCA.R, .direction = "downup") %>%
  fill(MCA.S, .direction = "downup") %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(-id)

master.7 <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-5.csv") %>%
  mutate(PersonID = as.integer(PersonID)) %>%
  left_join(el, by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(mca.highest, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(english.learner = ifelse(is.na(english.learner), 0, english.learner),
         Dem_Desc = fct_relevel(Dem_Desc, "Town/rural mix", "Urban/town/rural mix", "Entirely urban"))

assessments.master <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-5.csv") %>%
  select(PersonID) %>%
  mutate(PersonID = as.integer(PersonID)) %>%
  left_join(el, by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(mca.highest, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(english.learner = ifelse(is.na(english.learner), 0, english.learner))

write_csv(assessments.master, "Data/SLEDS/Masters/assessments_master.csv")

The dataset has 3,010,265 rows and 6 columns. Here are the columns and their definitions.

EnrollmentBeginTimeID: Begin date for the student’s period of attendance.
EnrollmentEndTimeID: End date for the student’s period of attendance.
OPEID: Office of Postsecondary Education (OPE)/FICE code of the college that the student attended (Foreign Key to IPEDSCharacteristics).
InstitutionName: Name of institution
EnrollmentStatus: The last enrollment status reported for the student. This field will have ‘N/A’ or “NULL” if the reporting college has not defined the student’s enrollment status as directory information. Here are the code definitions;

F: Full-time
Q: Three-quarter time
H: Half-time
L: Less than half-time
A: Leave of absence
W: Withdrawn
D: Deceased


Essentially, this dataset provides semester-based information - each observation is a semester/single period with the institutional information and beginning and end time of that single period (usually a semester). For example, if an individual attended South Dakota State University, attended in a “typical” fashion (fall and spring semesters), and graduated in 4 years, there would be 8 observations for that PersonID - one observation per semester.
There are a few pieces of information that I want to consolidate from this dataset;

Did the PersonID in the master dataset attend a college - yes or no?
Did the PersonID attend college during high school (PSEO), immediately after graduation or wait?
Did the PersonID attend multiple colleges - yes or no?
What type of college did the PersonID attend first?
Did the PersonID attend a public, private not-for-profit, or private or, for-profit college(s)?
At any point during their college career, did the PersonID attend a college(s) inside or outside of the Southwest Region or outside the EDR of their high school?

I was going to include the length of time that a PersonID attended college, but due to differences in how institutions report enrollment periods, it didn’t seem like it would be a great indicator.
The pieces of information missing in the original dataset is location and type of institution attended.To do this we will need to join the original dataset with an IPEDS dataset using opeid.
The IPEDS data and the NSC data will only match using the first 6 digits of the IPEDS OPEID values. So I will change that in the NSC data. Then I can join.


ipeds.original <- read_csv('/Users/kellyasche/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-kasche@ruralmn.org/My Drive/Research/FY25-27/FY26/OHE Journey to meaningful employment/Data/SLEDS/IPEDS/IPEDS.csv') 

ipeds.sector <- ipeds.original %>%
  filter(!is.na(OPEID)) %>%
  mutate(OPEID = str_pad(OPEID, width = 8, side = "left", pad = "0"),
         OPEID.6 = str_sub(OPEID, 1, 6)) %>%
  select(Unitid, OPEID.6, City, State, FIPS, GeographicRegion, CountyCode, InstitutionSector, InstitutionName)  %>%
  mutate(CountyCode = str_pad(CountyCode, width = 5, side = "left", pad = "0"))

nsc.enrollment.ipeds<- nsc.enrollment.original %>%
  left_join(ipeds.sector, by = "OPEID.6") %>%
  drop_na(Unitid) %>%
  mutate(EnrollmentStatus = as_factor(EnrollmentStatus))

Next we will determine thy type(s) of college(s) they attended during their post-secondary career. To do this we will first create a dataset with columns for each institution sector and a confirmation indicator on whether the PersonID attended that particular sector at some point in their career. I will then create a new category indicating that attended more than one type of institution sector. Once completed, I will be left with a dataset that has a column for each unique PersonID and what sector they attended, as well as a newly created code for “attended more than 1 type of sector”.


grad.list <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-8.csv") %>%
  select(PersonID)

nsc.enrollment.institution.types <- nsc.enrollment.ipeds %>%
  distinct(PersonID, InstitutionSector) %>%
  mutate(attended = 1) %>%
  complete(PersonID, InstitutionSector, fill = list(attended = 0)) %>%
  mutate(label = paste("ps.sector.", InstitutionSector, sep = "")) %>%

Next we will determine whether they attended a post-secondary institution inside or outside of the planning region, outside their EDR, or outside of Minnesota. Since many of the PersonID in the dataset have attended multiple institutions, we will categorize it in the following way in order to capture the combinations of attendance;

Attended inside region only (planning region, EDR, RUCA, State)
Attended inside and outside region (planning region, EDR, RUCA, state)
Attended outside region only (planning region, EDR, RUCA, state)

In order to do this we will need to combine our planning region and EDR joining documents with the nsc.enrollment.ipeds dataset. I need to remember that the way I arranged the regions are going to be different than the official planning region. We will also need to join the master dataset with it to determine the location of the PersonID’s high school graduation location. Lastly, we will need to join up the RUCA categories for counties outside of Minnesota. Then we can start the categorization process.

nsc.enrollment.location.join <- nsc.enrollment.ipeds %>%
  select(PersonID, InstitutionName, CountyCode) %>%
  left_join(dem.desc.county, by = c("CountyCode" = "State-County FIPS Code")) %>%
  left_join(grad.location, by = "PersonID") %>%
  drop_na(grad.ruca) %>%
  mutate(countyfp = str_sub(CountyCode, 3, 5),

  rename(ps.Dem_Desc = 4,

         ps.statefp = 9,

From here we can start creating new columns beginning with the RUCA category. to create this column we will gather each PersonID to examine whether or they attended a post-secondary institution in the same RUCA category, or if they attended multiple post-secondary institutions with one institution in the same category and another not the same.

  mutate(attended.ps.first.year = as.integer(str_sub(first.attend.ps, 1, 4)),

  left_join(nsc.enrollment.same.edr, by = "PersonID") %>%

attended.ps - this is a confirmation that the PersonID attended a post-secondary institution at some point after graduating high school.

ps.in.MN = did the PersonID attend a post-secondary institution in Minnesota.




Summary of students attending post-secondary
Lets summarize the percentage of students that attended a post-secondary institution and compare across RUCA categories.
Below is the percentage of students that attended a post-secondary institution from the entire dataset. 67% of the PersonIDs in the dataset attended a post-secondary institution at some point between 2007 and 2024.


attending.ps.pct.total <- master.9 %>%
  group_by(attended.ps) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) 

datatable(attending.ps.pct.total, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE,
          options = list(columnDefs = list(list(className = "dt-center", targets = 1:2)))) %>%
  formatCurrency(2, "", digits = 0) %>%
  formatPercentage(3)






Now lets check to see if this percentage is statistically significantly different by RUCA group.
The crosstabs do indicate that there is a statistically significant difference in the percentage of graduates that attend a post-secondary institution by high school RUCA category. The town/rural mix graduates attend post-secondary at a significantly lower rate than entirely urban and urban/town/rural mix graduates - 63.7%, compared to 70.7% and 67.7%, respectively.

The AP dataset has 283,151 observations and 5 columns. Each observation represents an AP exam taken so this means that a PersonID can be listed multiple times if the individual took multiple AP exams. The ExamGrade is on a 1 - 5 scale with the highest scores being better. According to Meredith at OHE, colleges give credit if the score is 3 or higher.
I’m a bit torn here. There seems to be three approaches to how I can utilize this data in the model.

I could either just create a category of whether an individual took an AP exam and not care what the grade was.
I could only use individuals who scored 3 or higher.
I could keep all the data and change it so that each observation represents a PersonID and new columns created for each AP exam and their score.

For now, I think I’m going to just utilize option 1 - whether they took an AP exam or not.

title: Employment
text:
Filter for “meaningful” employment
The biggest issue is how do we get a meaningful indicator on whether they were employed in the region and whether they are employed in an industry that matches their CTE experience that wasn’t just a “summer job”. We need to filter out summer jobs between college years, as well as adapt to different paths that students take.
We will define “meaningful employment” as an employment experience in which an individual works for one particular employer for 1,000 hours worked in any given year.
However, this isn’t going to just be checking to see if an individual has worked at an employer for 1,000 hours at graduation year, grad year +2, grad year +7 and grad year +12. Rather, it’s going to be checking on whether they are working at an employer at grad year, grad year +2, grad year +7 and grad year +12 for which they worked 1,000 hours for an given year.
For example, a person may be employed with an employer for a few years working full-time, but part-way through grad year +7, they decide to move on. I want to make sure we capture that that individual was employed in meaningful employment even though it wasn’t full-time that particular year.
The same can go the other way. Perhaps an individual just starts employment at grad year +7 but does work full-time with that particular employer form multiple years. We will want to count that as well.
In addition, I want to capture if someone is working at an employer but isn’t quite “meaningful” but turns into meaningful later on. We will count that as well.
This will be a couple step process.

First, we will filter out the employment.original data so that only meaningful employment for each PersonID is included along with the years worked at EmploymentOrganizationID.
Collect EmploymentOrganizationID for all the years that each PersonID worked meaningful employment.
Create a new datalist of each PersonID in the master datalist with grad year, grad year +2, and +7.
Then, we will cross reference the grad year list with employment year to see if meaningful employment matches.

We will end with the following columns and labels;

PersonID has had meaningful employment since graduating high school (Grad year, grad year +2, grad year +7)

No MN emp record - Has no MN emp record
No meaningful emp - Has MN emp record but never
Meaningful emp - Has MN emp record and is meaningful
After 2023 - the grad year +X is after 2023.




meaningful.employer <- employment.updated %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4))) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, EmploymentOrganizationID, CalendarYear) %>%
  summarize(EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked = sum(EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  filter(EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked > 999) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  distinct(PersonID, EmploymentOrganizationID) %>%
  right_join(mn.emp.record[,c(1)], by = "PersonID")

The dataset above provides each PersonID in our Master datalist along with a confirmation on whether they had meaningful employment on their graduation year, and grad year +2 and +7. As expected, there are 137,622 rows.

title: Employment
section: Match meaningful employment and high school locations/regions.
text:
Match meaningful employment and high school locations/regions.
Now, we want to determine if the locations of meaningful employment match the counties and regions from which they graduated high school. To do this, we will import the latest master dataset so we can compare their high school locations with meaningful employment locations.
Here are the columns and labels that I need;

PersonID has had meaningful employment within the county/region (Grad year, grad year +2, grad year +7)

No MN emp record - has no MN employment record
No meaningful emp - Has MN emp record but not meaningful
No location match - Has MN emp record, had meaningful employment, but no match with region
Location match - Has MN emp record, had meaningful employment, and had meaningful employment in county/region
After 2023 - the grad year +X is After 2023




emp.original.locations <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4)),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, " County", ""),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Saint Louis", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Duluth", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Minneapolis", "Hennepin"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of St. Paul", "Ramsey"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Shakopee Mdewakanton Community", "Scott"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "White Earth Tribal Counci", "Mahnomen")) %>%
  left_join(counties.regions.1, by = c("CountyName" = "Name")) %>%
  rename(EconomicDevelopmentRegionName = edr) %>%
  select(PersonID, CalendarYear, EmploymentOrganizationID, EconomicDevelopmentRegionName, CountyName, project.pr) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, CalendarYear, EmploymentOrganizationID, EconomicDevelopmentRegionName, CountyName, project.pr) %>%
  rename(employment.county = CountyName,
         emp.edr = EconomicDevelopmentRegionName,
         emp.pr = project.pr) %>%
  mutate(emp.edr = str_replace(emp.edr, "  ", " "),
         emp.edr = as.factor(emp.edr),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, " County", ""),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "City of Duluth", "St. Louis"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "Saint Louis", "St. Louis"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "City of Minneapolis", "Hennepin"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "City of St. Paul", "Ramsey"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "White Earth Tribal Counci", "Mahnomen"),
         employment.county = as.factor(employment.county)) %>%
  left_join(counties.regions[,c(2,4)], by = c("employment.county" = "Name")) %>%
  rename(emp.Dem_Desc = Dem_Desc) 

meaningful.emp.locations <- meaningful.emp.grad.years %>%
  left_join(emp.original.locations, by = c("PersonID", "year" = "CalendarYear", "EmploymentOrganizationID")) %>%
  mutate(emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)", "Unknown", as.character(emp.edr)),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)", "Unknown", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Hennepin", "EDR 11 - 7 County Twin Cities", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Ramsey", "EDR 11 - 7 County Twin Cities", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "St. Louis", "EDR 3 - Arrowhead", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Unknown", "Unknown", emp.edr),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "Unknown", "Unknown", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "NULL", "NULL", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Mahnomen", "EDR 2 - Headwaters", emp.edr))

grad.locations <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-10.csv") %>%
  mutate(planning.region = "Central") %>%
  select(PersonID, county.name, Dem_Desc, edr, planning.region) %>%
  rename(hs.county.name = county.name,
         hs.Dem_Desc = Dem_Desc,
         hs.edr = edr,
         hs.planning.region = planning.region)

grad.emp.location.match <- grad.locations %>%
  right_join(meaningful.emp.locations, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(county.match = ifelse(employment.county == hs.county.name, 1,
                               ifelse(employment.county %in%  c("Unknown", "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)"), 0, -1)),
         edr.match = ifelse(emp.edr == hs.edr, 1,
                            ifelse(emp.edr == "Unknown", 0, -1)),
         region.match = ifelse(emp.pr %in% c("Central"), 1,
                               ifelse(emp.edr == "Unknown", 0, -1)),
         state.match = 1) %>% 
  group_by(PersonID, grad.years) %>%
  summarize(county.match = max(county.match),
         edr.match = max(edr.match),
         region.match = max(region.match),
         state.match = max(state.match)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  gather(key = "region.match", value = "confirm", 3:6) %>%
  mutate(confirm = ifelse(confirm == -1, "No location match",
                          ifelse(confirm == 0, "Unknown", "Location match")),
         grad.years.region.emp.match = paste(grad.years, ".", region.match, sep = "")) %>%
  select(PersonID, grad.years.region.emp.match, confirm) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = grad.years.region.emp.match, values_from = confirm, values_fill = "No meaningful employment") %>%

title: Employment
section: Match employment industry with career cluster
text:
Match employment industry with career cluster
Next we need to find a way to compare the CTE careerclusters with the actual industry from which they work. We are not able to compare majors which is a bummer. But, the careerclusters from CTE coursework does align somewhat with NAICS codes. Here’s what it looks like;


careercluster.naics.cw <- read_xlsx('/Users/kellyasche/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-kasche@ruralmn.org/My Drive/Research/FY25-27/FY26/OHE Journey to meaningful employment/Data/SLEDS/Employment/career-cluster-naics.xlsx') %>%
  rename(cw.CareerCluster = `Career cluster code`,
         cw.CareerClusterName = `Career Cluster`,
         cw.emp.ind.code = 3,
         cw.emp.ind.name = 4)


datatable(careercluster.naics.cw, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE,
          options = list(columnDefs = list(list(className = "dt-center", targets = 1:3)))) 






There is one industry in which two career clusters will have to be marged - Human Services and Health Science & Health Occupations. Due to this, we will create a new column with an “updated” careercluster code that includes the merged cluster.
Here are the columns and labels that I will use;

PersonID has had meaningful employment in industry from a CTE course taken (Grad year, grad year +2, grad year +7)

No MN emp record - has no MN employment record
No meaningful emp - Has MN emp record nut not meaningful
No ind match - Has MN emp record, was meaningful, but industry does not match CTE course taken
Ind match - Has MN emp record, was meaningful, and industry and cTE course match.
After 2023 - the grad year +X is After 2023


Step 1 is to determine the industry codes for each PersonID that experienced meaningful employment for each of their “grad years”.


emp.original.for.cw <- employment.updated %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4))) %>%
  select(PersonID, CalendarYear, EmploymentOrganizationID, GroupCode) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, CalendarYear, EmploymentOrganizationID, GroupCode) 

cc.cw.meaningful.emp <- meaningful.emp.grad.years %>%
  left_join(emp.original.for.cw, by = c("PersonID", "EmploymentOrganizationID", "year" = "CalendarYear")) %>%
  mutate(ind.code = ifelse(GroupCode == "6215", "6215", str_sub(GroupCode, 1, 2)),
         ind.code = as.integer(ind.code)) %>%
  left_join(careercluster.naics.cw, by = c("ind.code" = "cw.emp.ind.code"))

Step 2 is to merge each PersonID’s cte courses taken. with the meaningful employment dataset so we can compare if the CTE courses match the industries.


grad.cc <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-10.csv") %>%
  select(PersonID, 22:46) %>%
  gather(key = "cte", value = "n.courses", 2:ncol(.)) %>%
  filter(n.courses > 0) %>%
  rename(cte.cw = cte) %>%
  select(PersonID, cte.cw, n.courses)

grad.cc.cw.naics <- cc.cw.meaningful.emp %>%
  left_join(grad.cc, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(cc.ind.match = ifelse(is.na(n.courses), -1,
                               ifelse(cw.CareerCluster == cte.cw, 1, 0)),
         cc.ind.match = ifelse(ind.code == 54, 1, cc.ind.match)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, grad.years) %>%
  summarize(max.match = max(cc.ind.match)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(cc.ind.match = ifelse(max.match == -1, "No CTE",
                               ifelse(max.match == 0, "No ind match", "Ind match")),
         cc.ind.match = ifelse(is.na(cc.ind.match), "No crosswalk", cc.ind.match)) %>%
  select(PersonID, grad.years, cc.ind.match) %>%
  complete(PersonID, grad.years) %>%
  mutate(label = paste("ind.match.", grad.years, sep = "")) %>%
  select(PersonID, label, cc.ind.match) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = label, values_from = cc.ind.match)

title: Employment
text:
County employment match
First, let’s look what percentage of individuals had an employment instance where the employer was located in the same county as their high school.
The table below shows that 13% of the individuals in the master dataset had meaningful employment in the same county as their high school the year they graduated. It increased to 17% two years after graduation and then 18% seven years after graduation. These percentages are after filtering out all of the “After 2023” category.


match.region.summary.total.county <- master.11 %>%
  select(PersonID, hs.grad.year.county.match, hs.grad.year.2.county.match, hs.grad.year.7.county.match) %>%
  gather(key = "hs.grad.year", value = "county.match", 2:4) %>%
  filter(county.match != "After 2023") %>%
  group_by(hs.grad.year, county.match) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(hs.grad.year) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(data_id = seq(n()),
         hs.grad.year = str_sub(hs.grad.year, 1, 14),
         hs.grad.year = str_replace(hs.grad.year, "hs.grad.year.c", "hs.grad.year"))

match.region.summary.total.county.plot <- ggplot(match.region.summary.total.county, aes(hs.grad.year, pct, fill = county.match, group = county.match)) +
  geom_col_interactive(position = "dodge", aes(data_id = data_id, tooltip = paste(hs.grad.year, "\nEmployment match high school county? - ", county.match, sep = ""))) +
  geom_label(aes(label = percent(pct, accuracy = .1)), show.legend = FALSE, color = "white", size = 5, position = position_dodge(width = .9)) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x="", y = "", color="", title = "Percent of individuals with meaningful employment in high school\ncounty")+
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent)+
  theme_bar+
  scale_fill_manual(values = brewer.pal(n = 6, "RdYlBu"),
                    guide = guide_legend(ncol = 3)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        text = element_text(size = 18))


girafe(ggobj = match.region.summary.total.county.plot, width_svg = 10, height_svg = 10) %>%
  girafe_options(opts_selection(type = "none"),
                 opts_sizing(rescale = FALSE))

Crosstabs indicate a relationship.

hs.grad.year: The more rural a district is, the higher the percentage of graduates that have meaningful employment in the high school county - 14.1% for town/rural mix vs. 8.9% for entirely urban.
hs.grad.year.2: The increasing percentage for rural districts continues - 18.8% for town/rural mix districts vs. 11.3% for entirely urban.
hs.grad.year.7: Same as previous years - 19.5% for town/rural mix vs. 10.3% for entirely urban.

Next we will look at the percentage of individuals that have meaningful employment in the EDR the year they graduate, two years after graduating, and seven years after graduating.
The chart below shows that 15.5% of individuals in the main dataset had meaningful employment in the edr the year of graduation. The percent increases to 25.3% of individuals seven years after graduating. All “After 2023” individuals were taken out.


match.edr.summary.total.edr <- master.11 %>%
  select(PersonID, hs.grad.year.edr.match, hs.grad.year.2.edr.match, hs.grad.year.7.edr.match) %>%
  gather(key = "hs.grad.year", value = "edr.match", 2:4) %>%
  filter(edr.match != "After 2023") %>%
  group_by(hs.grad.year, edr.match) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(hs.grad.year) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(data_id = seq(n()),
         hs.grad.year = str_sub(hs.grad.year, 1, 14),
         hs.grad.year = str_replace(hs.grad.year, "hs.grad.year.e", "hs.grad.year"))

match.edr.summary.total.edr.plot <- ggplot(match.edr.summary.total.edr, aes(hs.grad.year, pct, fill = edr.match, group = edr.match)) +
  geom_col_interactive(position = "dodge", aes(data_id = data_id, tooltip = paste(hs.grad.year, "\nEmployment match high school edr? - ", edr.match, sep = ""))) +
  geom_label(aes(label = percent(pct, accuracy = .1)), show.legend = FALSE, color = "white", size = 5, position = position_dodge(width = .9)) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x="", y = "", color="", title = "Percent of individuals with meaningful employment in edr")+
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent)+
  theme_bar+
  scale_fill_manual(values = brewer.pal(n = 6, "RdYlBu"),
                    guide = guide_legend(ncol = 3)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        text = element_text(size = 18))


girafe(ggobj = match.edr.summary.total.edr.plot, width_svg = 10, height_svg = 10) %>%
  girafe_options(opts_selection(type = "none"),
                 opts_sizing(rescale = FALSE))

Relationship confirmed for each timeyearX.
Interestingly, it shows that the more rural districts have a higher percentage of graduates that have meaningful employment in their EDR. By seven years after graduating, 17% of town/rural mix graduates had meaningful employment, compared to 16% for urban/town/rural mix, and 12.3% for entirely urban.

In the original dataset we have 4642670 rows and 16 columns. Below is a description of each variable.

PersonID: Identification for all individuals across datasets.
TimeID: Last day of of fiscal quarter
EmploymentOrganizationID: An internal identification for each employer.
EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked: The total number of hours worked by an employee at an employer’s location during a specific calendar quarter
EmployeeQuarterlyWages: The total wages earned by an employee at an employer’s location during a specific calendar quarter
EmployeeTenure: The total number of quarters a worker has been employeed by an organization at a specific location, up to an including the current calendar quarter
IndustryID: Auto generated ID code for a record in the Industry dimension.
USIndustryCode: Six-digit North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) code
GroupCode: Four-digit North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) code
OwnershipCode: A classification system based upon the controlling interest of the establishment primarily designed to distinguish between governmental and non-governmental establishments

10 = Federal government
20 = State government
30 = Local government
50 = Private

EmployerLocationTotalWagesPaid: The total wages paid to all workers employeed by an organization at a specific location during a specific calendar quarter
QuarterlyAverageEmployment: The average number of workers employeed by an organization at a specific location during a specific calendar quarter
County: Minnesota county code to which this institution belongs. This can be used as a foreign key into the Geography dimension on MNCounty.

Link to codes

CountyName: The name of the county corresponding to the County and MNCounty Codes for this Location.
MNCounty: County Code for this location as assigned by the state of Minnesota.

Link to codes City: All of the city data is NA

City: City location, which are blank and will be eliminated.

The next thing I want to do is put in the EDR and region of each of these employment instances. I will convert the “County” column to a 3 width character format and then match it with my counties.regions.1 list.


employment.updated <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(County = formatC(County, width = 3, flag = "0")) %>%
  left_join(counties.regions.1[,c(1,5,10)], by = c("County" = "countyfp"))

So all the previous datasets we structured and filtered so that each observation in the master dataset was an individual. We will want to continue to do the same. So we need to create an employment dataset with the following columns;

PersonID
High school graduation year
Whether the individual had an employment record the year of, and each subsequent year, of high school graduation.
How many years after graduation each employment check is (i.e. grad.year.1, grad.year.2,….etc.)





grad.years <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-10.csv") %>%
  select(PersonID, hs.grad.year)

mn.emp.record.year <- employment.updated %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4))) %>%
  select(PersonID, CalendarYear) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, CalendarYear) %>%
  mutate(mn.emp.record = "MN emp record") %>%
  filter(CalendarYear > 2007) %>%
  filter(CalendarYear < 2024) %>%
  complete(PersonID, CalendarYear, fill = list(mn.emp.record = "No MN emp record")) 

mn.emp.record <- grad.years %>%
  left_join(mn.emp.record.year, by = c("PersonID")) %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = ifelse(is.na(CalendarYear), hs.grad.year, CalendarYear),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(is.na(mn.emp.record), "No MN emp record", mn.emp.record),
         update = ifelse(CalendarYear < hs.grad.year, "Not graduated HS", "Graduated")) %>%
  filter(update == "Graduated") %>%
  select(!update) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  mutate(grad.year.seq = seq(n())) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  complete(PersonID, grad.year.seq) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  fill(hs.grad.year, .direction = "down") %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = ifelse(is.na(CalendarYear), hs.grad.year + (grad.year.seq - 1), CalendarYear),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(CalendarYear > 2023, "After 2023", mn.emp.record),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(is.na(mn.emp.record), "No MN emp record", mn.emp.record),
         grad.year = paste("grad.year.", grad.year.seq-1, sep = "")) %>%
  select(-grad.year.seq)

The dataset above provides each unique PersonID from our master list along with each possible grad year and subsequent years (grad.year.0, grad.year.1, grad.year.2 … grad.year.16).
Here is the logic;

grad.year.x > 2023: mn.emp.record == “After 2023”,
if there’s a MN employment record for the PersonID and the grad.year.x: mn.emp.record == “MN emp record”
if there’s no MN employment record for the PersonID and the grad.year.x: mn.emp.record == “No MN emp record”

There are 2,201,952 rows in this dataset with 137,622 individuals.




The biggest issue is how do we get a meaningful indicator on whether they were employed in the region and whether they are employed in an industry that matches their CTE experience that wasn’t just a “summer job”. We need to filter out summer jobs between college years, as well as adapt to different paths that students take.
We will define “meaningful employment” as an employment experience in which an individual works for one particular employer for 1,000 hours worked in any given year.
This will be a couple step process. First we will build a dataset that has each grad.year.x from each PersonID high school graduation year and match it with the MN employment records. We will end up with each PersonID having each grad.year.x along with wither they have a MN employment record, whether they had meaningful employment, whether grad.year.x is after 2023, or whether they have no MN employment record.


meaningful.employer <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4))) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, EmploymentOrganizationID, CalendarYear) %>%
  summarize(AnnualHoursWorked = sum(EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  right_join(mn.emp.record, by = c("PersonID", "CalendarYear")) %>%
  mutate(grad.year = fct_relevel(grad.year, "grad.year.0", "grad.year.1", "grad.year.2", "grad.year.3", "grad.year.4", "grad.year.5", "grad.year.6", "grad.year.7", "grad.year.8", "grad.year.9", "grad.year.10", "grad.year.11"),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(AnnualHoursWorked > 999, "Meaningful employment", mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(CalendarYear > 2023, "After 2023", new.mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(new.mn.emp.record == "MN emp record", "MN emp record - not meaningful", new.mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(mn.emp.record == "No MN emp record", "No MN emp record", new.mn.emp.record),
         meaningful.emp.code = ifelse(new.mn.emp.record == "Meaningful employment", 1, 0)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, CalendarYear) %>%
  filter(meaningful.emp.code == max(meaningful.emp.code)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  distinct(PersonID, grad.year, meaningful.emp.code, .keep_all = TRUE)

  left_join(mn.emp.record.year, by = c("PersonID")) %>%

         mn.emp.record = ifelse(is.na(mn.emp.record), "No MN emp record", mn.emp.record),
         update = ifelse(CalendarYear < hs.grad.year, "Not graduated HS", "Graduated")) %>%
  filter(update == "Graduated") %>%
  select(!update) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  mutate(grad.year.seq = seq(n())) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  complete(PersonID, grad.year.seq) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  fill(hs.grad.year, .direction = "down") %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = ifelse(is.na(CalendarYear), hs.grad.year + (grad.year.seq - 1), CalendarYear),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(CalendarYear > 2023, "After 2023", mn.emp.record),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(is.na(mn.emp.record), "No MN emp record", mn.emp.record),
         grad.year = paste("grad.year.", grad.year.seq-1, sep = "")) %>%
  select(-grad.year.seq)

The dataset above provides each unique PersonID from our master list along with each possible grad year and subsequent years (grad.year.0, grad.year.1, grad.year.2 … grad.year.16).
Here is the logic;

grad.year.x > 2023: mn.emp.record == “After 2023”,
if there’s a MN employment record for the PersonID and the grad.year.x: mn.emp.record == “MN emp record”
if there’s no MN employment record for the PersonID and the grad.year.x: mn.emp.record == “No MN emp record”

title: Employment states each year
text:
The biggest issue is how do we get a meaningful indicator on whether they were employed in the region and whether they are employed in an industry that matches their CTE experience that wasn’t just a “summer job”. We need to filter out summer jobs between college years, as well as adapt to different paths that students take.
We will define “meaningful employment” as an employment experience in which an individual works for one particular employer for 1,000 hours worked in any given year.
This will be a couple step process. First we will build a dataset that has each grad.year.x from each PersonID high school graduation year and match it with the MN employment records. We will end up with each PersonID having each grad.year.x along with wither they have a MN employment record, whether they had meaningful employment, whether grad.year.x is after 2023, or whether they have no MN employment record.


meaningful.employer <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4))) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, EmploymentOrganizationID, CalendarYear) %>%
  summarize(AnnualHoursWorked = sum(EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  right_join(mn.emp.record, by = c("PersonID", "CalendarYear")) %>%
  mutate(grad.year = fct_relevel(grad.year, "grad.year.0", "grad.year.1", "grad.year.2", "grad.year.3", "grad.year.4", "grad.year.5", "grad.year.6", "grad.year.7", "grad.year.8", "grad.year.9", "grad.year.10", "grad.year.11"),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(AnnualHoursWorked > 999, "Meaningful employment", mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(CalendarYear > 2023, "After 2023", new.mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(new.mn.emp.record == "MN emp record", "MN emp record - not meaningful", new.mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(mn.emp.record == "No MN emp record", "No MN emp record", new.mn.emp.record),
         meaningful.emp.code = ifelse(new.mn.emp.record == "Meaningful employment", 1, 0)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, CalendarYear) %>%
  filter(meaningful.emp.code == max(meaningful.emp.code)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  distinct(PersonID, grad.year, meaningful.emp.code, .keep_all = TRUE)
