This dataset has 64,382 rows and 6 columns. Here are explanations of the rows:

Graduated: Whether the student graduated. This dataset only provides students that have a “Y” in the column.
GraduationTimeID: Provides the yearmonthday of the PersonID graduation.
OPEID: ID of the institution which has been converted to an 8 long string padded with “0” on the left.
InstitutionName: Name of the institution from which the PersonID graduated.
DegreeTitle: The Degree Title the PersonID graduated with. This column is a shitshow - some have values of BA, while others have it written out - Bachelor of Arts. I will need to fix this.
Major - Major the PersonID graduated with.
OPEID.6 - this is the OPEID with a string length of 6 so that it matches up with our IPEDS dataset.

The main characteristics from this dataset that I want to add to the master dataset/model are the following;

Confirmation that they graduated from a post secondary institution
The year they graduated from their first post secondary institution
The year they graduated from their last post-secondary institution
The sector of the institution(s) from which they graduated
The highest level of degree obtained by the PersonID
The degrees earned
Whether the institution(s) from which they graduated are in the same RUCA category, EDR, planning region, and state as their high school

Okay, lets first create a dataset with a unique PersonID and a column confirming that they graduated from a post secondary institution. However, we don’t want to include any students that never had a chance to complete their post-secondary institution. For example, if an individual has graduated by 2023 (the last year of the data), but is attending, then they shouldn’t be counted against the region for not having that person not “graduated”.
Essentially, what we want to identify is that in 2023, has the individual;

Graduated from a post-secondary institution,
Is still attending post-secondary institution,
Not attending post-secondary and never graduated from one.

To do this, I will need to import the NSC enrollment data, filter to 2023, and double check to see if anyone in our graduate list was attending post-secondary that year. Then ps.grad can be categorized as the following;

ps.grad: graduated from a post-secondary institution by 2023
ps.attending: attending post-secondary as of 2023
not.ps.grad: never graduated from a post-secondary institution and wasn’t enrolled in one as of 2023.

title: Pathway Descriptions
text: This project adopts a pathways-based framework to summarize patterns of workforce participation observed among Central Minnesota high school graduates. These pathways were not defined a priori, but instead emerged through repeated and consistent patterns observed across multiple analytic approaches, including descriptive distributions of workforce states over time, cross-tabulation analyses of individual characteristics, predictive CART models, and focused subgroup and persistence analyses. Across these methods, individuals clustered into three analytically distinct groups based on employment intensity, geographic location of employment, and stability over time. The pathways framework is used here as an organizing device to synthesize these findings and to describe patterned relationships between educational experiences and workforce outcomes. The pathways do not represent deterministic life courses, nor do they imply individual intent or preference; rather, they summarize observed regularities in administrative data and provide a structured way to discuss how characteristics and institutional pathways are associated with different workforce participation outcomes.

title: Pathway Descriptions
text: This project adopts a pathways-based framework to summarize patterns of workforce participation observed among Central Minnesota high school graduates. These pathways were not defined a priori, but instead emerged through repeated and consistent patterns observed across multiple analytic approaches, including descriptive distributions of workforce states over time, cross-tabulation analyses of individual characteristics, predictive CART models, and focused subgroup and persistence analyses. Across these methods, individuals clustered into three analytically distinct groups based on employment intensity, geographic location of employment, and stability over time. The pathways framework is used here as an organizing device to synthesize these findings and to describe patterned relationships between educational experiences and workforce outcomes. The pathways do not represent deterministic life courses, nor do they imply individual intent or preference; rather, they summarize observed regularities in administrative data and provide a structured way to discuss how characteristics and institutional pathways are associated with different workforce participation outcomes.

title: Pathway Descriptions
text:
Anchored Pathway

Definition
The Anchored Pathway consists of individuals who achieve Sustained WF – Region, defined as working 1,000 or more hours for a single employer within the Central Minnesota region in a calendar year at observed points after high school. This pathway is defined strictly by employment intensity and geographic location and does not imply long-term residence, preference, or immobility.


Characteristics

Demographic
Individuals in the Anchored Pathway are more likely to be male than female. Demographic characteristics alone do not determine pathway membership, but gender differences become more pronounced in analyses that focus on non-postsecondary graduates.


High School Characteristics
Participation in career-aligned or CTE coursework is strongly associated with the Anchored Pathway. This association appears consistently across cross-tabulation analyses and emerges as a protective routing factor in CART models, particularly for individuals without four-year postsecondary credentials.


High School Accomplishments / Academic
Higher academic preparation, particularly higher GPA, is associated with increased representation in Sustained WF – Region. Among non-college graduates, higher GPA is associated with both earlier entry into sustained regional employment and greater persistence once achieved. The Anchored Pathway is not associated with the lowest academic performance, but rather with moderate to strong preparation that does not route individuals into four-year postsecondary pathways.


Post-Secondary
The Anchored Pathway includes two primary postsecondary profiles: individuals with no postsecondary attendance and individuals who complete a two-year credential, particularly when earned from a postsecondary institution located within the region. Completion of four-year credentials, especially outside the region, is consistently associated with movement away from this pathway.


Strength of Associations
The strongest associations with the Anchored Pathway are postsecondary pathway type (no postsecondary or two-year credential) and location of postsecondary institution (in-region). Career-aligned high school coursework is the next strongest factor, appearing repeatedly in both associative and predictive analyses. Academic preparation acts as a conditioning factor that influences entry and persistence but is secondary to postsecondary pathway structure.



Narrative
The Anchored Pathway reflects a pattern of stable, region-based employment that is strongly associated with locally oriented educational trajectories. Individuals in this pathway either enter the workforce directly after high school or complete two-year, regionally located postsecondary credentials. Career-aligned high school experiences and solid academic preparation increase both access to and durability within this pathway. Among non-college graduates, sustained regional employment is not fragile when supported by appropriate high school preparation.

title: Pathway Descriptions
text:
Mobility Pathway

Definition
The Mobility Pathway consists of individuals who achieve Sustained WF – MN outside the Central Minnesota region or who have no Minnesota employment record during the observation period. This pathway captures sustained employment occurring outside the region and does not indicate weak labor force attachment.


Characteristics

Demographic
Demographic variables play a limited role in predicting membership in the Mobility Pathway once educational characteristics are accounted for. Differences by gender narrow substantially after postsecondary pathways are introduced.


High School Characteristics
High school characteristics matter primarily insofar as they support academic signaling that enables postsecondary enrollment. These characteristics do not independently predict mobility without postsecondary mediation.


High School Accomplishments / Academic
High academic achievement is a defining upstream characteristic of the Mobility Pathway. Higher GPA, standardized test participation, and advanced coursework consistently route individuals into four-year postsecondary pathways.


Post-Secondary
Four-year postsecondary pathways are the strongest and most consistent predictor of the Mobility Pathway. Completion of four-year credentials, particularly from institutions located outside the region, sharply reduces the likelihood of Sustained WF – Region and increases the likelihood of Sustained WF – MN or absence from Minnesota employment records.


Strength of Associations
Four-year postsecondary participation is the dominant association underlying the Mobility Pathway and appears as the first and most decisive split in predictive models. Academic preparation is a strong upstream factor, operating primarily through postsecondary routing rather than directly influencing employment geography.



Narrative
The Mobility Pathway reflects a structured sequence in which strong academic preparation routes individuals into four-year postsecondary education, followed by sustained employment outside the Central Minnesota region or outside Minnesota altogether. Mobility outcomes are therefore not residual or weakly connected outcomes, but the predictable result of educational sorting that begins in high school and is crystallized through four-year postsecondary participation.

title: Pathway Descriptions
text:
Weakly Connected to Pathways

Definition
The Weakly Connected group consists of individuals who have a Minnesota employment record but do not meet the threshold for Sustained WF, defined as fewer than 1,000 hours with a single employer in a calendar year. This group reflects lower-intensity or unstable workforce participation rather than non-participation.


Characteristics

Demographic
Female individuals are more likely than male individuals to appear in this group, particularly among non-college graduates. These differences persist over time rather than converging.


High School Characteristics
Lack of career-aligned or CTE coursework is a strong risk factor for remaining in Non-sustained WF. Individuals with minimal exposure to career-aligned pathways are more likely to both enter and persist in this group.


High School Accomplishments / Academic
Lower academic preparation, including lower GPA and limited participation in standardized testing or advanced coursework, is strongly associated with Non-sustained WF. Among non-college graduates, these academic differences are associated with persistent weak connection rather than temporary instability.


Post-Secondary
The Weakly Connected group is more common among individuals with no postsecondary attendance or with postsecondary attempts that do not result in credential completion. Attempted postsecondary education without completion does not appear to mitigate risk and, in some cases, is associated with greater employment churn.


Strength of Associations
The strongest associations with the Weakly Connected group are lack of postsecondary credential completion and weak academic preparation. Career-aligned coursework functions as a key protective factor, while demographic characteristics primarily condition outcomes rather than drive them.



Narrative
The Weakly Connected group represents a persistent pattern of lower-intensity workforce participation within Minnesota. This group is not defined by a single transition period, but by continued difficulty achieving sustained employment over time. Without strong academic preparation or access to career-aligned pathways, individuals are more likely to remain weakly connected to the workforce.

title: Pathway Descriptions
text:
Key Takeaways and Implications
Workforce participation outcomes among Central Minnesota graduates reflect structured educational and employment pathways rather than isolated individual choices. The Anchored Pathway is supported by locally oriented educational routes, particularly career-aligned high school experiences and two-year, in-region postsecondary credentials. The Mobility Pathway is driven by four-year postsecondary education and reflects educationally mediated geographic employment patterns. The Weakly Connected group is characterized by persistent non-sustained employment associated with weaker academic preparation and limited access to career-aligned pathways.
From a policy perspective, these findings suggest that no single intervention will influence all outcomes. High school–level levers, particularly career-aligned coursework and academic preparation, are critical for individuals who do not pursue four-year postsecondary education. Postsecondary system alignment, especially the role of two-year and in-region institutions, is central to sustaining regional workforce participation. Mobility outcomes should not be interpreted solely as regional loss, but as part of a broader educational and labor market system in which different pathways respond to different institutional signals and opportunities.

title: Dependent Variables States
text:
There are many paths in which an individual can take after graduating high school. What we are most concerned with is whether an individual has “meaningful” employment, when and where this employment takes place, and are there any variables that are associated with each of these pathways.
The paths that we want to identify are the following;

Meaningful employment

Meaningful employment - same county as high school
Meaningful employment - same EDR as high school, but not the same county
Meaningful employment - in Central Minnesota, but not in the same EDR as their high school
Meaningful employment - in Minnesota, but not in Central Minnesota

Not meaningful employment or no MN Employment record - attending post-secondary
Not meaningful employment - not attending post-secondary
No MN employment record - not attending post-secondary

We are going to assess each PersonID on which of those pathways they are at the time of their high school graduation, and each subsequent year up to 2023.

The dataset has 729,218 rows and 6 columns. Here are the columns and their definitions.

EnrollmentBeginTimeID: Begin date for the student’s period of attendance.
EnrollmentEndTimeID: End date for the student’s period of attendance.
OPEID: Office of Postsecondary Education (OPE)/FICE code of the college that the student attended (Foreign Key to IPEDSCharacteristics).
InstitutionName: Name of institution
EnrollmentStatus: The last enrollment status reported for the student. This field will have ‘N/A’ or “NULL” if the reporting college has not defined the student’s enrollment status as directory information. Here are the code definitions;

F: Full-time
Q: Three-quarter time
H: Half-time
L: Less than half-time
A: Leave of absence
W: Withdrawn
D: Deceased


Essentially, this dataset provides semester-based information - each observation is a semester/single period with the institutional information and beginning and end time of that single period (usually a semester). For example, if an individual attended South Dakota State University, attended in a “typical” fashion (fall and spring semesters), and graduated in 4 years, there would be 8 observations for that PersonID - one observation per semester.
The primary pieces of information I want from this dataset is each year a PersonID was attending a post-secondary institution. So let’s shrink the dataset down to just the following columns;

PersonID
unique year attending a post-secondary institution

The PersonID will be filtered using the EnrollmentStatus variable equaling full-time, three-quarter time, half-time, and less than half-time.
For the unique year, it won’t matter how many semesters they were attending. If an individual attended half a year, then worked full-time, my meaningful employment definition should pick it up and transfer it into that category. Otherwise, they will be in the category - attending post-secondary with no meaningful employment or no MN employment record.


ps.attend.year <- nsc.enrollment.original %>%
  filter(EnrollmentStatus %in% c("F", "H", "Q", "L", "NULL")) %>%
  mutate(begin.year = str_sub(EnrollmentBeginTimeID, 1,4),
         end.year = str_sub(EnrollmentEndTimeID, 1, 4)) %>%
  select(PersonID, begin.year, end.year) %>%
  gather(key = "BeginOrEnd", value = "year", 2:3) %>%
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, year) %>%
  rename(ps.attend.year = year) %>%
  mutate(ps.attend = "ps.attend")

We now have a dataset that provides the employment state and a confirmation on post-secondary attendance for each PersonID and grad.year.x.
Let’s analyze.



Proportion of individuals per path by grad.year.x
Next we want to figure out the different paths that these group of individuals take. The paths that we are most interested in are the following;

After 2023
Has meaningful employment in same county as high school
Has meaningful employment in same EDR as high school, but not same county
Has meaningful employment in Southwest Minnesota, but not in same EDR as high school.
Has meaningful employment in Minnesota, but not in Southwest Minnesota.
Does not have meaningful employment or a MN employment record, but is attending post-secondary
Does not have meaningful employment and is not attending post-secondary.
Does not have a MN employment record and is not attending post-secondary.

Let’s first build a new dataset where each PersonID has one of these seven states for each grad.year.x.


seven.states <- ps.emp.states %>%
  mutate(states = ifelse(county.match == "Meaningful emp - match", 1, 99),
         states = ifelse(edr.match == "Meaningful emp - match" & county.match != "Meaningful emp - match", 2, states),
         states = ifelse(region.match == "Meaningful emp - match" & county.match != "Meaningful emp - match" & edr.match != "Meaningful emp - match", 3, states),
         states = ifelse(state.match == "Meaningful emp - match" & county.match != "Meaningful emp - match" & edr.match != "Meaningful emp - match" & region.match != "Meaningful emp - match", 4, states),
         states = ifelse(state.match == "After 2023", 0, states),
         states = ifelse(ps.attend == "ps.attend" & !(states %in% c(0,1,2,3,4)), 5, states),
         states = ifelse(ps.attend == "ps.not.attend" & state.match == "MN emp record - not meaningful", 6, states),
         states = ifelse(ps.attend == "ps.not.attend" & state.match == "No MN emp record", 7, states),

The new dataset has 2,201,952 rows and 10 with 137,622 unique individuals. The seven states are labeled as the following;

Meaningful emp County: means they have worked 1,000 hours or more for one employer located in the same county as their high school.
Meaningful emp EDR: means that have worked 1,000 hours or more for one employer located in the same EDR as their high school, but not in the same county.
Meaningful emp SW: means they have worked 1,000 hours or more for one employer located in Southwest Minnesota, but not in the same EDR or county as their high school.
Meaningful emp MN - means they have worked 1,000 hours or more for one employer located in Minnesota, but not in Southwest Minnesota.
Attending ps: Means the individuals either has a MN employment record but it isn’t meaningful OR they do not have a MN employment record, but they are attending post-secondary.
Not meaningful, not attending ps: this means they do have a MN employment record, but it isn’t meaningful and they are not attending post-secondary.
No MN emp record - not attending ps: this means they do not have a MN employment record nor are they attending a post-secondary institution.

The other designation is “After 2023” which will be filtered out whenever I analyze the dataset.
Let’s first take a look at the proportion of individuals that are in each state at each grad.year.x.
The chart below shows the proportion of individuals in the dataset that are in each “state/path” for each grad.year.x. There are a couple of things to highlight.

The percentage of individuals with meaningful employment in Central Minnesota peaks about 6 years after college with nearly a quarter of graduates working 1,000 hours or more that year for a single employer.
At 6 years after graduating, over half of the graduates have meaningful employment in Minnesota.
Graduates not reaching the meaningful employment threshold in Minnesota hovers around 15% after the first year of graduating high school.
Nearly 30% of graduates disappear from my dataset about 10 years after graduating. This means they are not going to post-secondary in the United States and do not have a Minnesota employment record.

text:
Independent Variables
To maintain interpretability and avoid overfitting, analysis will include a limited set of theoretically and empirically important predictors identified in earlier analyses:

Strongest predictors

Postsecondary

High school characteristics

Variables were selected based on:

Strength of association in prior bivariate analyses
Policy relevance
Conceptual clarity
Avoidance of redundant or highly collinear measures

These variables represent the full set of predictors examined across a series of structured logistic regression models. They are not entered simultaneously; rather, postsecondary variables are evaluated in separate specifications to avoid redundancy and to isolate distinct mechanisms (attainment depth, institutional sector, and geographic completion location).
High school contextual variables (EDR, rural classification, county unemployment, county wages) are excluded due to consistently weak relationships in earlier analyses.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Logistic Regression
text:
Modeling Strategy
Rather than estimating a single fully saturated model, predictors are introduced in a structured sequence to evaluate distinct mechanisms and to assess coefficient attenuation across specifications. This staged approach strengthens interpretability and reduces redundancy among highly related postsecondary variables.

Model 1: Structural and Preparation Baseline
The first model includes demographic and high school preparation variables:

RaceEthnicity
economic.status
SpecialEdStatus
pseo.participant
ACTCompositeScore
ap.exam
MCA.comp score (single strongest or composite measure)
cte.achievement
Dem_Desc
avg.wages.pct.state

This baseline model evaluates whether structural background and academic readiness are independently associated with sustained regional employment.


Model 2: Educational Attainment Mechanism
The second model introduces:

highest.cred.level

This model tests whether credential depth explains regional attachment beyond preparation and demographic factors. Changes in coefficients from Model 1 to Model 2 are examined to assess attenuation and potential shared pathway mechanisms.


Model 3: Institutional Pathway Mechanism
In a separate specification, credential level may be replaced with:

ps.grad.InstitutionSector

This model evaluates whether type of postsecondary institution (e.g., 2-year public, 4-year public, other) is associated with regional workforce retention, independent of preparation factors.


Model 4: Geographic Completion Mechanism
A final specification introduces:

ps.grad.location

This model tests whether completing postsecondary education within the region is associated with sustained regional employment, holding other factors constant. Given prior findings, graduation location is expected to be one of the strongest predictors.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Logistic Regression
text:
Evaluation Criteria
Results will be reported using:

Odds ratios
95% confidence intervals
Statistical significance levels
Directional interpretation

Model comparison metrics (AIC and pseudo R²) will be used to assess relative improvement across specifications, but emphasis will remain on coefficient stability and magnitude rather than overall model fit.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Logistic Regression
text:
Interpretation Framework
Interpretation will focus on:

Direction and relative magnitude of associations
Changes in coefficients across models
Evidence of attenuation when postsecondary variables are introduced

Findings will be described as associations holding other included variables constant. No causal claims will be made.
This structured approach allows for evaluation of three central mechanisms underlying sustained regional employment:

Preparation (academic readiness and early college exposure)
Attainment depth (credential level)
Geographic and institutional pathway (where and how postsecondary education was completed)

Together, these models provide multivariate confirmation of patterns identified in earlier descriptive analyses while preserving conceptual clarity and interpretability.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Logistic Regression
section: Model 1 - Demographics, HS Characteristics, HS Accomplishments
text:
Model 1 - Demographics, HS Characteristics, HS Accomplishments
Model 1 serves as the baseline structural and preparation model, estimating the association between demographic background, high school academic preparation, and sustained regional employment five years after graduation. This specification excludes postsecondary attainment variables in order to isolate whether early academic readiness and structural characteristics independently differentiate workforce pathway outcomes. By modeling these predictors first, the analysis establishes whether observed disparities in regional workforce attachment emerge prior to postsecondary completion.
This baseline model tests the preparation mechanism: whether differences in academic proficiency and early college or career exposure are associated with sustained regional employment, holding structural background constant. Subsequent models will introduce postsecondary variables to assess whether these preparation effects persist, attenuate, or are mediated through educational attainment and geographic completion pathways.
Model 1 estimates the association between demographic characteristics and high school academic preparation with sustained regional employment five years after graduation, prior to the inclusion of postsecondary attainment variables. This baseline specification isolates whether early readiness and exposure pathways independently differentiate regional workforce attachment.
The model retains nearly the full analytic sample, with only 2,990 observations removed due to MCA Math missingness.
Racial and ethnic disparities remain substantial:

Black students: approximately 48–50% lower odds of sustained regional employment relative to White students.
Asian/PI students: roughly 36% lower odds.
American Indian students: about 31% lower odds.
Hispanic students: approximately 23% lower odds.

These disparities persist even after accounting for academic preparation and structural context.
Academic mobility indicators show a consistent outward orientation pattern:

Higher MCA Math scores: associated with lower odds of sustained regional employment (~6% lower odds per unit increase), suggesting that academically stronger students are more likely to pursue opportunities outside the region.
AP participation: strongly associated with lower regional attachment (~39% lower odds).
PSEO participation: small negative association (~5% lower odds), modest in magnitude.

Career-aligned coursework shows clearer positive associations than in prior specifications:

CTE concentrators/completers: approximately 16% higher odds of sustained regional employment.
CTE participants: roughly 14% higher odds.

These effects are stronger than in earlier ACT-based models, suggesting that CTE operates independently of standardized academic proficiency.
Structural place factors remain meaningful:

Entirely urban high schools: roughly 50% lower odds of sustained regional employment relative to town/rural mix schools.
Urban/town/rural mix schools: modestly lower odds relative to the reference category.
Higher local wages (avg.wages.pct.state): associated with lower regional attachment, though more modestly than urbanicity.

Economic disadvantage and Special Education status show relatively small independent associations once preparation and place are included.
Overall, Model 1 indicates that sustained regional employment in Central Minnesota reflects a combination of structural place context, persistent racial disparities, modest academic mobility patterns, and a clearer positive role for CTE participation. The mobility gradient associated with academic proficiency and advanced coursework remains evident, while CTE shows a distinct association with regional workforce attachment.

    RaceEthnicity +

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Logistic Regression
text:
Model 2: Adding Postsecondary Attainment
Model 2 extends the baseline specification by introducing postsecondary credential attainment (highest.cred.level) to assess whether high school preparation effects persist once educational completion is held constant. This model tests the attainment mechanism: whether differences in sustained regional employment reflect variation in credential level rather than solely high school readiness or demographic background.
By adding credential level, the analysis evaluates whether previously observed associations—particularly those related to CTE participation, math proficiency, PSEO participation, and race/ethnicity—attenuate when postsecondary attainment is accounted for. If coefficients for preparation variables shrink substantially, this would suggest that their influence operates indirectly through educational attainment. Conversely, if effects remain stable, this would indicate that preparation and attainment independently shape regional workforce retention. Model 2 therefore clarifies whether credential depth mediates, partially explains, or leaves unchanged the structural and preparation patterns observed in Model 1.
Model 2 introduces postsecondary credential level and substantially improves model fit (AIC decreases from 85,890.63 to 85,148.30), indicating that credential attainment explains meaningful additional variation in sustained regional employment beyond demographics, preparation, and place context.
Credential level emerges as a central differentiator:

Associate degree: approximately 62% higher odds of sustained regional employment relative to non-graduates.
Less than Associate degree: roughly 57% higher odds.
Bachelor’s degree or higher: about 23% lower odds relative to non-graduates.

This pattern reinforces a clear regional workforce pipeline tied to sub-baccalaureate credentials, while four-year completion is associated with outward mobility.
CTE effects remain positive and slightly stronger than in Model 1:

CTE concentrators/completers: ~11% higher odds.
CTE participants: ~11% higher odds.

Importantly, CTE maintains an independent association even after controlling for credential level, indicating that its relationship with regional employment is not fully mediated through postsecondary attainment.
Academic mobility indicators continue to show outward orientation:

Higher MCA Math scores: associated with lower odds (~5% lower odds per unit increase).
AP participation: strongly negative (~33% lower odds).
PSEO participation: no longer statistically meaningful once credential level is included.

Racial and ethnic disparities persist:

Black students: ~48% lower odds.
Asian/PI students: ~36% lower odds.
American Indian students: ~30% lower odds.
Hispanic students: ~23% lower odds.

Structural place context remains influential:

Entirely urban schools: ~50% lower odds relative to the reference category.
Urban/town/rural mix schools: modestly lower odds (~11%).
Local wage context: no longer statistically distinct once credentials are included.

Overall, Model 2 clarifies that sustained regional employment in Central Minnesota is strongly shaped by sub-baccalaureate credential attainment, while four-year pathways align with outward mobility. CTE continues to function as a modest but independent workforce-alignment mechanism, and academic proficiency remains associated with geographic mobility rather than regional retention. Persistent racial disparities remain evident even after accounting for credential level and preparation.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Logistic Regression
text:
Model 3: Geographic Completion Mechanism
Model 3 extends the prior specification by incorporating the location of postsecondary completion (ps.grad.location) alongside credential level. This model tests the geographic completion mechanism: whether sustained regional employment is associated not only with the depth of educational attainment, but also with where that education was completed.
By including graduation location, the analysis distinguishes between two related but conceptually distinct pathways. Credential level captures human capital depth, while graduation location captures regional attachment and institutional embeddedness. This specification evaluates whether the strong retention effects observed for associate-level credentials in Model 2 reflect the nature of the credential itself or the geographic proximity of the institution attended.
Model 3 therefore assesses whether regional graduation exerts an independent association with sustained regional employment, and whether the inclusion of geographic completion attenuates previously observed effects for credential level, CTE participation, and demographic characteristics. If coefficients for credential level shrink meaningfully, this would suggest that geographic embeddedness plays a central role in shaping long-term regional workforce retention.
Model 3 introduces postsecondary graduation location and substantially improves model fit (AIC decreases from 85,148.30 to 82,938.66), indicating that geographic completion explains a large additional share of variation in sustained regional employment beyond credential level and preparation factors.
Graduating from a postsecondary institution within the region emerges as the dominant predictor:

PS grad region: approximately 235% higher odds of sustained regional employment relative to non-graduates (OR ≈ 3.35).
PS grad outside MN: about 35% lower odds.
PS grad MN (non-regional): not statistically distinct from non-graduates.

This sharply reinforces the central importance of regional institutional embeddedness rather than degree attainment alone.
Once location is included, credential-level effects largely attenuate:

Associate degree and less than Associate degree: no longer statistically distinct from non-graduates.
Bachelor’s degree or higher: associated with ~44% lower odds of sustained regional employment.

This shift indicates that prior positive effects of sub-baccalaureate credentials were largely operating through where the credential was earned.
CTE remains independently associated with regional retention:

CTE concentrators/completers: ~12% higher odds.
CTE participants: ~11% higher odds.

These effects persist even after accounting for both credential level and graduation location, suggesting that CTE functions as a direct workforce-alignment mechanism rather than solely through postsecondary geography.
Academic mobility indicators continue to align with outward pathways:

Higher MCA Math scores: modestly lower odds (~3% per unit increase).
AP participation: ~30% lower odds.
PSEO participation: not statistically distinct.

Structural and demographic disparities remain substantial:

Black students: ~49% lower odds.
Asian/PI students: ~36% lower odds.
American Indian students: ~30% lower odds.
Hispanic students: ~21% lower odds.
Entirely urban schools: ~46% lower odds.
Urban/town/rural mix schools: ~10% lower odds.
Economic disadvantage: ~10% lower odds.

Overall, Model 3 makes the mechanism clear: sustained regional employment in Central Minnesota is primarily driven by graduating from a postsecondary institution within the region. Credential level alone does not drive retention once geography is accounted for. CTE remains a consistent, modest independent contributor, while higher academic achievement and four-year pathways are associated with outward mobility. Persistent racial disparities remain evident even after controlling for educational pathway and geographic completion.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Logistic Regression
text:
Model 4: Institutional Sector × Geographic Completion
Model 4 replaces credential level with a combined institutional sector × graduation location specification in order to disentangle sector effects from geographic embeddedness. This model provides the strongest overall fit and clarifies that sustained regional employment is driven by the interaction between institutional type and where the credential was earned.
Model 4 replaces credential level with the combined institutional sector × graduation location specification and provides the strongest overall fit (AIC decreases from 82,938.66 to 82,823.96), indicating that sector-specific geographic embeddedness explains additional variation beyond location alone.
Graduating from a postsecondary institution within the region remains the dominant predictor, now differentiated by sector:

2-year public, PS grad region: approximately 207% higher odds of sustained regional employment (OR ≈ 3.07).
4-year public, PS grad region: approximately 142% higher odds (OR ≈ 2.42).
Other institutional type, PS grad region: approximately 70% higher odds (OR ≈ 1.70).

This confirms that regional embeddedness matters across sectors, but most strongly for 2-year public institutions.
Graduating outside the region is consistently associated with outward mobility:

4-year public, PS grad outside MN: approximately 61% lower odds (OR ≈ 0.39).
Other institutional type, PS grad outside MN: approximately 62% lower odds (OR ≈ 0.38).
2-year public, PS grad outside MN: approximately 41% lower odds (OR ≈ 0.59).

Within Minnesota but outside the region, patterns vary:

2-year public, PS grad MN (non-regional): modest positive association (~15% higher odds).
4-year public and other institutional types, PS grad MN: substantially lower odds (roughly 40–50% lower).

These patterns clarify that the strongest retention pathway is local completion at 2-year public institutions, while four-year and non-regional pathways align with mobility.
CTE remains independently associated with regional retention:

CTE concentrators/completers: ~12% higher odds.
CTE participants: ~11% higher odds.

These effects persist even after accounting for detailed sector and location categories, reinforcing CTE as a direct workforce-alignment mechanism rather than solely a pipeline into regional colleges.
Academic mobility indicators continue to align with outward pathways:

Higher MCA Math scores: modestly lower odds (~3% per unit increase).
AP participation: ~30% lower odds.
PSEO participation: not statistically distinct.

Structural and demographic disparities remain pronounced:

Black students: ~49% lower odds.
Asian/PI students: ~36% lower odds.
American Indian students: ~30% lower odds.
Hispanic students: ~21% lower odds.
Entirely urban schools: ~47% lower odds.
Urban/town/rural mix schools: ~11% lower odds.
Economic disadvantage: ~9% lower odds.

Overall, Model 4 makes the mechanism even clearer than Model 3: sustained regional employment in Central Minnesota is primarily driven by completing a credential within the region, especially at 2-year public institutions. Sector matters, but geography matters more. CTE remains a consistent, modest independent contributor, while higher academic achievement and four-year pathways—particularly outside the region—are associated with outward mobility. Persistent racial and structural disparities remain evident even after controlling for detailed educational pathways and geographic completion.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Logistic Regression
text:
Multivariate Confirmation Summary
Across progressively specified logistic regression models, sustained regional employment in Central Minnesota is driven primarily by postsecondary geography and institutional embeddedness, with high school CTE participation operating as a consistent but secondary pathway. Academic preparation variables play a more modest and often mobility-aligned role once postsecondary pathways are accounted for.
Key Findings

Graduating from a 2-year public institution within the region is associated with approximately 207% higher odds of sustained regional employment (OR ≈ 3.07). This is the single strongest predictor in the final model.
Graduating from a 4-year public institution within the region is associated with approximately 142% higher odds (OR ≈ 2.42).
Graduating from other institutional types within the region is associated with roughly 70% higher odds (OR ≈ 1.70).
In contrast, graduating from institutions outside the region is strongly associated with outward mobility:

4-year public outside MN: ~61% lower odds.
Other institutional types outside MN: ~62% lower odds.
2-year public outside MN: ~41% lower odds.

Graduating from a 2-year public institution elsewhere in Minnesota (non-regional) shows a modest positive association (~15% higher odds), while 4-year and other non-regional MN completions are associated with substantially lower odds.
CTE participation remains independently associated with regional retention across all specifications:

CTE concentrators/completers: ~12% higher odds.
CTE participants: ~11% higher odds.


These effects persist even after accounting for detailed sector × location pathways, indicating that CTE functions as a direct workforce-alignment mechanism rather than merely channeling students into regional colleges.

Academic mobility indicators align with outward pathways:

Higher MCA Math scores: modestly lower odds (~3% per unit increase).
AP participation: ~30% lower odds.
PSEO participation: not statistically distinct in final models.

Structural disparities remain substantial:

Black students: ~49% lower odds.
Asian/PI students: ~36% lower odds.
American Indian students: ~30% lower odds.
Hispanic students: ~21% lower odds.
Entirely urban schools: ~47% lower odds.
Urban/town/rural mix schools: ~11% lower odds.
Economic disadvantage: ~9% lower odds.


Overall Interpretation
Two mechanisms shape sustained regional employment in Central Minnesota.
First, regional postsecondary embeddedness is the dominant driver. Completing a credential within the region—especially at a 2-year public institution—dramatically increases the likelihood of long-term regional workforce attachment. Geography explains far more variation than credential level alone. Once sector × location is modeled jointly, it becomes clear that retention is not simply about earning a degree; it is about where that degree is earned.
Second, CTE participation operates as a consistent, independent alignment pathway. Although its magnitude is modest relative to postsecondary geography, it remains statistically robust across all models. This suggests that structured career pathways in high school contribute directly to regional workforce attachment rather than functioning solely through postsecondary completion.
In contrast, higher academic achievement and four-year pathways—particularly outside the region—are associated with mobility rather than retention. Academic readiness appears to facilitate broader opportunity structures that extend beyond the region.
Even after accounting for preparation, credential attainment, institutional sector, and geographic completion, racial and structural disparities remain pronounced, indicating that educational pathways alone do not fully explain differences in sustained regional workforce attachment.
Overall, the Central Minnesota results point to a clear pipeline: high school career alignment (CTE) and, most decisively, regional postsecondary completion—particularly through 2-year public institutions—anchor individuals to the regional labor market. Mobility-oriented academic pathways and non-regional completion, by contrast, align with outward workforce trajectories.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Logistic Regression
text:
Big Takeaways
1. Regional postsecondary embeddedness is the dominant workforce retention mechanism.
Graduating from a postsecondary institution within the region is the single strongest predictor of sustained regional employment.

2-year public × regional graduation: ~207% higher odds (OR ≈ 3.07).

4-year public × regional graduation: ~142% higher odds (OR ≈ 2.42).

Other institutional types × regional graduation: ~70% higher odds (OR ≈ 1.70).

These are large, stable, and substantively decisive effects. Once sector × geography is specified, credential level alone no longer explains retention—where the degree is earned matters far more than what degree is earned.

2. CTE operates as a modest but consistent independent pathway.
Across all workforce models—including those controlling for credential level and sector × location—CTE remains positively associated with sustained regional employment:

CTE concentrators/completers: ~12% higher odds.

CTE participants: ~11% higher odds.

However, when modeling regional postsecondary graduation, CTE shows little association with in-region completion. This indicates that CTE’s workforce effect does not operate primarily through regional college graduation. Instead, it appears to function as a more direct workforce-alignment mechanism.
In Central, CTE matters—but it is not the dominant driver. Geography is.

3. Four-year and non-regional pathways align with outward mobility.
Graduating outside the region is consistently associated with lower odds of sustained regional employment:

4-year public outside MN: ~61% lower odds.

Other institutional types outside MN: ~62% lower odds.

2-year public outside MN: ~41% lower odds.

Bachelor’s degree attainment is associated with lower regional retention once geography is considered. This indicates that higher-degree pathways—especially when completed outside the region—function as mobility channels rather than regional anchors.

4. Academic readiness aligns more with mobility than retention.
Higher MCA Math scores and AP participation are associated with lower odds of sustained regional employment in workforce models. In the regional graduation model, MCA shows minimal association, and PSEO is strongly associated with regional graduation (~56% higher odds).
This pattern suggests:

Academic readiness facilitates postsecondary progression.
But it does not anchor students regionally.
Higher academic pathways likely expand geographic opportunity rather than reinforcing local retention.


5. Structural disparities emerge at graduation and persist into workforce outcomes.
Racial and structural inequalities are evident in both regional graduation and regional employment models.
In workforce models:

Black students: ~49% lower odds.

Asian/PI students: ~36% lower odds.

American Indian students: ~30% lower odds.

Hispanic students: ~21% lower odds.

In regional graduation models:

Hispanic students: ~53% lower odds of regional graduation.

American Indian students: ~43% lower odds.

Asian/PI students: ~25% lower odds.

Black students: not statistically distinct once controls are included.

Economic disadvantage, Special Education status, and entirely urban school context are also strongly associated with lower odds of regional graduation and lower odds of sustained regional employment.
These disparities are not eliminated by controlling for credential level, institutional sector, or graduation location. Structural inequality remains embedded throughout the pipeline.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Logistic Regression
text:
Overall Conclusion
Sustained regional employment in Central Minnesota is shaped primarily by locally embedded postsecondary institutions—especially 2-year public colleges—combined with modest but consistent contributions from CTE pathways.
Credential attainment alone does not drive retention. Geography does.
Academic readiness expands opportunity but does not anchor students regionally. Four-year and non-regional pathways align with outward mobility. CTE contributes independently but at a smaller magnitude than in some other regions.
Most importantly, structural disparities appear early in regional postsecondary graduation and persist into workforce outcomes. Educational pathway differences explain part of regional retention, but they do not fully account for persistent racial and socioeconomic gaps.
In short, Central Minnesota’s workforce retention pipeline is geographically anchored, institutionally embedded, modestly reinforced by career-aligned high school preparation, and constrained by enduring structural inequality.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Non-college grads
text:
Study Population
The analytic sample is restricted to individuals who did not complete a postsecondary credential. This restriction isolates workforce dynamics among high school graduates entering the labor market directly.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Non-college grads
text:
Outcome Variable
The primary model predicts:

Sustained employment – region (binary outcome)

The dependent variable is coded as:

1 = Sustained employment – region
0 = All other workforce outcomes (including sustained employment – MN outside the region, non-sustained employment, and no MN employment record)

This specification maintains consistency with earlier modeling while isolating mechanisms specific to the non-college population.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Non-college grads
text:
Independent Variables
Because postsecondary mechanisms are not applicable in this subgroup, the model focuses on high school preparation, structural background, and local labor market context identified as important in earlier analyses.
Predictors include:

High school accomplishments

cte.achievement
total.cte.courses.taken (if applicable)
pseo.participant
MCA.M
ap.exam

Demographic characteristics

RaceEthnicity
economic.status
SpecialEdStatus

High school and local context

Dem_Desc
avg.wages.pct.state
avg.unemp.rate (if included)


Variables are selected based on:

Strength of association in prior subgroup analyses
Conceptual plausibility within a non-college pathway
Policy relevance
Avoidance of redundancy

Postsecondary variables are excluded by design.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Non-college grads
text:
Time-Based Modeling Strategy
Workforce attachment evolves over time. To capture this dynamic process, models will be estimated separately at:

1 year after high school
5 years after high school
10 years after high school

This staged approach allows examination of how mechanisms change across early, mid-term, and longer-term workforce trajectories.

Year 1: Immediate Labor Market Entry
The 1-year model captures early transition into the labor market. At this stage, high school preparation and career alignment are expected to exert the strongest influence. CTE exposure and intensity may function as immediate workforce anchors, while structural disadvantage may strongly shape early labor market attachment.


Year 5: Stabilization Phase
The 5-year model reflects early career consolidation. At this point, initial preparation effects may attenuate, and differences associated with labor market context and structural disadvantage may become more pronounced. This model evaluates whether early alignment persists or whether structural conditions increasingly shape outcomes.


Year 10: Long-Term Embeddedness
The 10-year model captures longer-term workforce integration. Earlier analyses suggest that local labor market conditions (e.g., wages and unemployment) may become more dominant over time. This specification tests whether contextual economic factors increasingly explain sustained regional employment among non-college graduates as individual preparation effects diminish.
Estimating separate models at each time point allows for:

Evaluation of coefficient stability over time
Assessment of attenuation or amplification of predictors
Identification of shifting mechanisms from individual preparation to structural context

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Non-college grads
text:
Modeling Strategy
Within each time period, predictors are introduced in a structured sequence:

Model 1: Structural and Preparation Baseline
Includes demographic and high school preparation variables:

RaceEthnicity
economic.status
SpecialEdStatus
cte.achievement
pseo.participant
MCA.M - dropped due to systemic missingness
ap.exam
Dem_Desc



Model 2: Local Labor Market Context
Adds contextual labor market measures:

avg.wages.pct.state
avg.unemp.rate (if applicable)

This specification evaluates whether labor market context attenuates or reinforces preparation effects.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Non-college grads
text:
Evaluation Criteria
Results will be reported using:

Odds ratios
95% confidence intervals
Statistical significance levels
Directional interpretation

Model comparison metrics (AIC and pseudo R²) will be used to assess relative improvement across specifications, but emphasis will remain on coefficient magnitude and stability across time.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Non-college grads
text:
Interpretation Framework
Interpretation will focus on:

Whether CTE retains independent influence across time
Whether structural disadvantage grows or attenuates
Whether labor market context becomes increasingly dominant
How mechanisms shift from Year 1 to Year 10

Findings will be described as associations holding other included variables constant. No causal claims will be made.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Non-college grads
text:
Conceptual Focus
For non–postsecondary graduates, this time-structured modeling framework evaluates three evolving mechanisms:

Career alignment at labor market entry
Structural advantage or disadvantage shaping early stability
Local economic opportunity structures influencing long-term embeddedness

Together, these models clarify whether sustained regional employment among non-college graduates reflects early career alignment, structural inequality, changing economic context, or a combination of all three across time.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Non-college grads
text:
Model 1 - Demographics, HS Accomplishments
Model 1 serves as the baseline structural and preparation model, estimating the association between demographic background, high school academic preparation, and sustained regional employment one year after graduation. This specification excludes the local labor market variables in order to isolate whether early academic readiness and demographic characteristics independently differentiate workforce pathway outcomes. By modeling these predictors first, the analysis establishes whether observed disparities in regional workforce attachment emerge prior to postsecondary completion.
CTE Pathways
CTE emerges as the strongest positive predictor in the model:

CTE Concentrator/Completor: ~42% higher odds of sustained regional employment (OR ≈ 1.42).
CTE Participant: ~26% higher odds (OR ≈ 1.26).

This indicates that structured career pathways in high school are strongly associated with immediate regional workforce attachment among non-college graduates.
Academic Acceleration

AP participation: ~20% lower odds (OR ≈ 0.80).
PSEO participation: not statistically distinct (OR ≈ 0.98).

Academic acceleration indicators do not promote regional retention in the non-college population and, in the case of AP, are associated with lower regional attachment.
Demographic and Structural Factors
Substantial disparities are evident:

American Indian students: ~44% lower odds (OR ≈ 0.56).
Asian/PI students: ~39% lower odds (OR ≈ 0.61).
Black students: ~39% lower odds (OR ≈ 0.61).

This model examines predictors of sustained regional employment five years after high school among individuals who did not complete postsecondary education. Model fit improves meaningfully over the null model (AIC ≈ 51,560), indicating that demographic and preparation variables explain a nontrivial share of variation in regional attachment at Year 5.
CTE Pathways
CTE remains the strongest positive predictor:

CTE Concentrator/Completor: ~22% higher odds of sustained regional employment (OR ≈ 1.22).
CTE Participant: ~23% higher odds (OR ≈ 1.23).

PSEO participation: not statistically distinct (OR ≈ 0.96).

Disparities remain substantial and in some cases intensify by Year 5:

Black students: ~51% lower odds (OR ≈ 0.49).
Asian/PI students: ~51% lower odds (OR ≈ 0.49).
American Indian students: ~38% lower odds (OR ≈ 0.62).
Hispanic students: ~25% lower odds (OR ≈ 0.75).
Special Education status: ~12% lower odds (OR ≈ 0.88).
Economic disadvantage: ~8% lower odds (OR ≈ 0.92).

Racial disparities appear stronger at Year 5 than at Year 1, suggesting widening divergence in sustained regional workforce attachment over time.
School Context

Entirely urban schools: ~48% lower odds (OR ≈ 0.52).
Urban/town/rural mix schools: ~11% lower odds (OR ≈ 0.89).

Urban school context remains a pronounced structural correlate of lower regional retention.
Overall Interpretation
By five years after high school, sustained regional employment among non-postsecondary graduates continues to be shaped primarily by CTE participation, with modest but consistent positive effects. Academic acceleration pathways remain unrelated or negatively related to regional attachment. Structural racial disparities persist and in some cases strengthen, and graduates of entirely urban schools are substantially less likely to exhibit sustained regional employment. The mechanism for this population appears stable over time: career-aligned preparation supports regional retention, while structural inequalities remain deeply embedded.

Local wage context is not statistically meaningful at 10 years (OR ≈ 1.06), and its inclusion does not attenuate any major coefficients. Overall, the 10-year results mirror the 1- and 5-year findings: CTE participation remains a durable positive pathway into sustained regional employment, AP participation aligns with outward mobility, and structural disparities by race and urban context persist across a decade of workforce participation. The stability of coefficients across models suggests these mechanisms are deeply embedded rather than short-term transitional effects.

  grad.year.10 ~
    RaceEthnicity +
    economic.status +
    SpecialEdStatus +
    pseo.participant +
    ap.exam +
    cte.achievement +
    Dem_Desc +
    avg.wages.pct.state,
  family = binomial,
  data = master.model.10
)

title: Post-secondary Paths CART
text:
Postsecondary Graduation Location (ps.grad.location)
Across all three modeling scenarios we’ve explored — comparing meaningful employment in the region to employment in Minnesota, to not meaningful employment, and to no Minnesota employment record — ps.grad.location consistently emerged as one of the most important predictors.
Graduating from a postsecondary institution within the region was strongly associated with a higher likelihood of being meaningfully employed in the region, suggesting that geographic alignment between educational attainment and local labor markets fosters stronger employment ties.
Graduating outside the region, particularly outside Minnesota, was linked with an increased likelihood of either securing meaningful employment elsewhere or having no Minnesota employment record at all.
These patterns point to the potential “stickiness” of local graduates in the regional workforce, and the challenges of retaining graduates who leave to complete their education.

title: Post-secondary Paths CART
text:
Highest Credential Level (highest.cred.level)
highest.cred.level was a dominant predictor in multiple models, particularly when distinguishing between individuals who were meaningfully employed in the region and those who were not.
Earning an associate degree or higher — and especially a bachelor’s degree or higher — was linked with greater odds of being meaningfully employed in the region.
Lower levels of attainment, including “some college” without a credential, “less than associate degree,” or “no college,” were associated with higher rates of disconnectedness (no Minnesota employment record, not attending postsecondary) or employment outside the region.
This reinforces the central role of credential attainment in improving employment stability and alignment with regional labor needs.

For both of these variables, we will combine classifications in order to have a smaller set to model against;

ps.grad.location

PS grad region
PS grad outside region: includes all individuals that graduated from college outside of the region.
Did not graduate ps

highest.cred.level

Associate degree or lower
Bachelors or higher
Did not graduate: includes individuals with some college and no college experience.



master <- master.original %>%
  mutate(ps.grad.location.new = ifelse(ps.grad.location %in% c("PS grad MN", "PS grad outside MN"), "PS grad outside region", as.character(ps.grad.location)),
         highest.cred.level.new = ifelse(highest.cred.level %in% c("Associate degree", "Less than Associate Degree"), "Associate degree or lower", as.character(highest.cred.level)),
         highest.cred.level.new = ifelse(highest.cred.level.new %in% c("No college", "Some college"), "Did not graduate ps", as.character(highest.cred.level.new)))

The idea here is to allow the decision tree to grow fully and observe the CP value. There are two methods for identifying the CP code;

Use the cp value with the lowest xerror from the base model.

title: Post-secondary Paths CART
text:
Main takeaway
Main Splits

The first and most influential split is PSEO participation. Individuals who did not participate in PSEO are much more likely to fall into the “Did not graduate PS” category. Among non-PSEO participants, the next split is Race/Ethnicity (AI/Black/Hispanic/Unknown vs. other groups), followed by Special Education status and Economic status. For PSEO participants, the main split is also Race/Ethnicity (AI/Unknown vs. other groups), followed by Economic status, and then ACT Composite Score thresholds (< 21, < 22, < 26) along with average wages as a percent of state average. These combinations differentiate between “Did not graduate PS,” “PS grad outside region,” and “PS grad region.”
Variable Importance

PSEO participation – Primary driver of the first split, strongest influence overall.
Race/Ethnicity – Consistent second-level split on both sides of the tree.
Economic status – Influential in both PSEO and non-PSEO branches.
ACT Composite Score – Multiple threshold splits influence postsecondary graduation location.
Special Education status – Key split for non-PSEO students from certain racial/ethnic groups.
Average wages (relative to state) – Smaller role, only relevant in a limited branch.

Interpretation Participation in PSEO strongly predicts likelihood of postsecondary graduation and whether it occurs within the high school region. Students without PSEO experience tend to have lower postsecondary graduation rates, especially those from underrepresented racial/ethnic groups, with special education needs, or from lower economic backgrounds. For students with PSEO experience, ACT score thresholds and economic status further refine the likelihood of regional versus non-regional graduation. Higher ACT scores are associated with greater odds of graduating outside the region, while economic disadvantages tilt toward non-completion. Wage levels relative to the state average only appear as a predictor in a narrow subgroup, suggesting it’s not a major factor overall.
Brief Conclusion The model shows that PSEO participation is the most significant factor in predicting postsecondary graduation location, with race/ethnicity, economic status, and ACT performance providing additional differentiation. Non-PSEO participants—especially from underrepresented racial/ethnic groups and lower economic backgrounds—are much more likely not to graduate. Among PSEO participants, academic performance and economic status determine whether graduation is more likely to occur within or outside the high school region.

title: Post-secondary Paths CART
text:
Main takeaway
Main Splits The most influential split is PSEO participation. Students without PSEO experience are more likely not to graduate from postsecondary education, while those with PSEO experience show higher rates of earning a bachelor’s degree or higher. For non-PSEO participants, the next split is Race/Ethnicity (Asian/PI/Black/Hispanic/White vs. others), followed by ACT Composite Score thresholds (≥ 21 and ≥ 26), with economic status and CTE achievement further refining outcomes. For PSEO participants, ACT Composite Score (≥ 20) is the initial determinant, followed by Race/Ethnicity, economic status, and Special Education status. In some branches, lower ACT scores (< 24) and special education status predict much higher rates of non-completion.
Variable Importance

PSEO participation – Strongest driver of overall classification, key root split.
ACT Composite Score – Appears multiple times with different thresholds (18, 20, 21, 24, 26), strongly differentiating educational outcomes.
Race/Ethnicity – Consistent second-level split, shaping degree level expectations.
Economic status – Important in both PSEO and non-PSEO paths, associated with lower completion at higher credential levels.
CTE achievement – Plays a smaller but notable role for high-scoring non-PSEO students.
Special Education status – Particularly important for lower ACT PSEO students.

Interpretation PSEO participation sharply divides the likelihood of postsecondary credential attainment. Non-PSEO students—particularly from certain racial/ethnic groups and with lower ACT scores—are far more likely to not graduate, while higher ACT scores and favorable economic conditions increase the odds of earning bachelor’s degrees. For PSEO students, ACT performance remains a strong determinant, with high scorers more likely to reach bachelor’s or higher credentials, and low scorers—especially those from disadvantaged economic backgrounds or with special education status—more likely not to complete. CTE achievement provides a modest boost in certain high-performing, non-PSEO cases.
Brief Conclusion The model underscores PSEO participation and ACT performance as the two most critical predictors of highest credential earned, with race/ethnicity, economic status, and—more selectively—CTE achievement and special education status providing additional nuance. High ACT scores combined with PSEO participation strongly favor bachelor’s-level attainment, while low scores, economic disadvantage, and lack of PSEO participation correspond with non-completion.

Key Patterns & Comparative Insights
1. Strongest Predictors of Outcome Differences

SpecialEdStatus and economic.status had the largest effect sizes, especially one year after graduation. Both were associated with lower postsecondary participation and greater disconnection from meaningful work, with disparities that persisted across a decade.
These two variables reflect structural barriers — economic and learning support — that strongly shape early and long-term outcomes.

2. Language-Related Variables

Both english.learner and non.english.home showed moderate effects early on.
Students with these language indicators were less likely to attend postsecondary and more likely to appear in disconnected categories.
While gaps narrowed over time, persistent differences suggest long-term barriers related to language acquisition and access.

3. Gender

Gender had a moderate short-term effect that decreased over time.
Males were more likely to take local employment, while females were more likely to attend postsecondary.
The gap gradually narrowed but did not fully disappear even after 10 years.

4. RaceEthnicity

Despite its importance, race/ethnicity had weaker statistical associations than other factors.
However, group-level disparities — especially for AI, Black, and Hispanic graduates — were consistent.
Asian/PI students showed unique patterns of early postsecondary participation and underrepresentation in local employment, possibly due to out-of-state or non-traditional career paths.

5. COVID-era Graduation

Graduation year relative to COVID had a statistically significant but weak effect.
Post-COVID grads were less likely to attend PS and more likely to work locally, likely due to pandemic-era constraints.

Conclusion
Among all the demographic variables, economic disadvantage and special education status emerged as the most powerful and persistent predictors of postsecondary and employment outcomes. Language and gender also played meaningful roles, particularly in the short term, while race/ethnicity and COVID-era graduation had weaker but still important associations.
These findings suggest that interventions aiming to improve post-high school pathways should prioritize support for low-income students, students receiving special education, and multilingual or English learner populations, especially in the critical first years after graduation.

title: Local Employment Cross-tabs
text:
Gender

Key Findings

There is a statistically significant relationship between gender and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ² = 2083.575, df = 4, Cramer’s V = 0.127, p < .001
5 years after graduation: χ² = 612.448, df = 4, Cramer’s V = 0.081, p < .001
10 years after graduation: χ² = 278.976, df = 4, Cramer’s V = 0.073, p < .001


The strength of association is moderate in the first year and diminishes over time to a weak but still significant relationship by year ten.


Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Females are more likely to be attending postsecondary education (55.3% vs. 43.7%), while males are more likely to be employed — especially within their high school region (15.3% vs. 10.9%). Males also have higher rates of no MN employment record (11.9% vs. 7.7%). These early differences reflect a pattern in which males enter the local workforce more often, while females pursue longer-term educational pathways.
5 Years After Graduation: Postsecondary enrollment declines across the board, but differences remain. Males continue to have higher rates of regional employment and are slightly more likely to be employed meaningfully somewhere in MN. The gender gap in disconnected outcomes narrows, suggesting some convergence over time.
10 Years After Graduation: Differences persist but are smaller. Males still maintain an edge in meaningful employment — both in-region and statewide — while females are slightly more likely to appear in the “no MN record” group, possibly due to moving out of state or untracked employment.


Conclusion
Gender-based differences are most pronounced in the first year, with males more likely to take local employment routes and females more likely to pursue postsecondary education. Over time, the differences narrow but remain, especially in terms of where employment is located and whether individuals are tracked in the MN employment system.

text:
economic.status

Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between economic status and post-graduation outcomes:

1 year after graduation: χ² = 7116.172, df = 4, Cramer’s V = 0.235, p < .001
5 years after graduation: χ² = 1409.165, df = 4, Cramer’s V = 0.122, p < .001
10 years after graduation: χ² = 373.783, df = 4, Cramer’s V = 0.085, p < .001

The strength of association is moderate to strong in the first year and gradually weakens over time, though differences persist.


Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Students not eligible for free/reduced lunch were far more likely to attend postsecondary education (57.4% vs. 32.6%). Students from low-income backgrounds were more likely to be employed locally in their high school region (16.2% vs. 11.7%) and more likely to be disconnected — either in non-meaningful roles (28.5%) or lacking MN employment records (13.5%).
5 Years After Graduation: Gaps narrow slightly but remain. Higher-income students continue to show higher rates of meaningful MN employment, while low-income students maintain elevated disconnection and are more concentrated in regional jobs, likely reflecting limited mobility or economic necessity.
10 Years After Graduation: Regional employment rates are similar, but higher-income students are still more likely to have meaningful jobs elsewhere in MN and less likely to be disconnected. The long-term trend suggests that early disparities in education and employment compound over time, even as the gap narrows.


Conclusion
Economic status is a powerful predictor of early postsecondary and employment outcomes. Students from low-income backgrounds are more likely to take local jobs out of necessity, less likely to pursue postsecondary education, and more vulnerable to long-term disconnection from the workforce. While disparities decrease by year ten, they remain meaningful.

title: Local Employment Cross-tabs
text:
SpecialEdStatus

Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between SpecialEdStatus and post-graduation outcomes across all three years:

1 year after graduation: χ² = 3177.82, df = 4, Cramer’s V = 0.248, p < .001
5 years after graduation: χ² = 1091.37, df = 4, Cramer’s V = 0.145, p < .001
10 years after graduation: χ² = 366.90, df = 4, Cramer’s V = 0.084, p < .001

The strength of association is strongest one year after graduation and diminishes over time, though remains statistically significant even ten years later.


Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Students who received special education services in high school were substantially less likely to be attending postsecondary education (only 1,375 compared to 24,769 peers without special ed status) and more likely to be in non-meaningful or untracked employment categories, including “no MN employment record” and “not meaningful” employment. While some were employed locally (838 in-region), the disparities suggest substantial barriers to immediate postsecondary success.
5 Years After Graduation: The gap narrows but persists. Special education students still trail their peers in postsecondary enrollment and are less likely to hold meaningful employment in MN (1,068 vs. 11,204) or in their local region (1,529 vs. 9,866). They are overrepresented in non-meaningful and no-record categories, though many do gain some form of employment by this point.
10 Years After Graduation: By year ten, special education students continue to be underrepresented in meaningful MN employment (1,373 vs. 14,267) and more likely to have no MN employment record or to be in a non-meaningful status. Postsecondary participation is negligible for both groups at this point. The long-term pattern reflects lasting disparities in workforce outcomes, though gaps are smaller than in earlier years.


Conclusion
Special education status is strongly associated with post-graduation outcomes, especially in the first year. Students with special education histories are consistently less likely to attend post secondary education and more likely to experience disconnection from the workforce over time. While some individuals do gain meaningful regional or statewide employment, the long-term opportunity gap remains, pointing to the need for sustained support well beyond high school.

title: Local Employment Cross-tabs
text:
RaceEthnicity

Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between race/ethnicity and post-graduation outcomes at all time points:

1 year after graduation: χ² = 719.74, df = 16, Cramer’s V = 0.059, p < .001
5 years after graduation: χ² = 352.07, df = 16, Cramer’s V = 0.041, p < .001
10 years after graduation: χ² = 301.57, df = 16, Cramer’s V = 0.038, p < .001

The association is statistically significant but weak at each time point and decreases slightly over time.


Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: White graduates were the most likely to be attending postsecondary education (24,849), while other groups — especially American Indian (AI) and Hispanic students — were more likely to be in non-meaningful employment or have no MN employment record. White students also had the highest counts in regional meaningful employment (5,742), while the counts for all other groups were much lower.
5 Years After Graduation: The overall pattern persists. White graduates had higher levels of meaningful MN employment and regional employment, while American Indian, Black, and Hispanic graduates were more concentrated in non-meaningful or disconnected categories. Postsecondary enrollment declined across all groups, but disparities in employment outcomes remained.
10 Years After Graduation: Postsecondary attendance was nearly zero across the board. White graduates continued to lead in meaningful MN and regional employment, while American Indian, Black, and Hispanic graduates had higher rates of disconnection (no MN record or not meaningful employment). The differences were smaller than in earlier years but still evident.


Conclusion
Racial and ethnic differences in post-graduation outcomes are present across all time points, though the overall effect size is weak. White graduates are consistently more likely to be enrolled in postsecondary education and employed meaningfully in both statewide and local contexts, while graduates identifying as American Indian, Black, or Hispanic are overrepresented in disconnected and non-meaningful employment categories. These patterns persist over time, albeit with diminishing strength, highlighting enduring disparities in opportunity and access.
